plos-pone-0004804:
Nora Lawo, Felix Wäckers, and Jörg Romeis reported that Indian Bt cotton varieties do not affect performance of cotton aphids, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cotton varieties expressing Cry proteins from Bacillus thuringiensis are grown worldwide for management of pest moths. To prevent non target pest outbreaks and retain biological control by predators and parasitoids. Effects on other insects must be checked carefully before and after commercial release.

Aphids are a key non target herbivore on cotton. The study found no effect of Bt varieties on aphid performance. That supports the specificity of the technology. Continued monitoring remains prudent in farming practice.
plos-pone-0005404:
Polyphosphate is an ancient chain of phosphate units, tens to hundreds long, joined by high-energy bonds. It forms complexes with many proteins and modulates their activity. Zakharian and colleagues asked what it does to TRPM8, the cold-sensing channel, in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Inorganic polyphosphate modulated TRPM8 channel function in their tests. A simple polymer tuning the body's cold sensor adds a control layer to temperature sensation. The result also hints at how energy-rich phosphate stores might adjust other ion channels. Cold sense guards us from frost and burn alike,. A plain chain of phosphates as its dial hints that the most old parts of the cell still run some of its most fine-tuned senses.
plos-pone-0005504:
Michael Miksa and co-authors studied sepsis in rats for a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Sepsis is a whole-body inflammation that can follow infection and damage organs. Early in sepsis, the stress hormone noradrenaline rises and can make immune cells react too strongly.

The team found that one receptor for the hormone, on immune cells in the gut, plays a central role in driving organ harm. Blocking that path may calm the harmful response. The work names a target for future sepsis drugs, an area where new options are badly needed. Sepsis still kills many patients in intensive care, so any firm drug target in the pathway draws close attention.
plos-pone-0005604:
Rosa Molfetta and co-authors studied how allergy receptors are removed from cell surfaces in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Tagging surface receptors with ubiquitin often sends them to be destroyed, quieting their signals. The IgE receptor, central to allergy, sits on mast cells and is tagged quickly when it meets its trigger.

The team showed that the tagging happens in special fat-rich patches of the cell surface. Adapter proteins that read the tags then pull the receptor inside. Blocking that removal could be a new way to calm allergic responses. Mast cells drive hay fever and asthma attacks, so their receptor handling is watched closely by drug teams.
plos-pone-0005704:
Jaklien Leemans and co-authors examined in 2009 how a sensor protein drives damage in failing kidneys. Long-term kidney disease brings swelling and scar tissue, called fibrosis, until the organ stops working. The sensor, toll-like receptor 2, sits in kidney tissue and can be set off by the body's own alarm signals.

The team followed the sensor's role as injury deepened over time. Their work links TLR2 to both the swelling and the scarring that follow. Blocking that sensor could slow the slide toward kidney failure. The study gives that idea a firm base in animal evidence.
plos-pone-0005804:
Maria Marchetti and co-authors reported in 2009 that a common anti-inflammatory drug makes cancer cells easier to kill under oxidative stress. Sulindac, an approved NSAID, blocks enzymes that make prostaglandins. It has long drawn interest for preventing colon polyps and cancer.

Under stress from reactive oxygen, sulindac-treated cancer cells died more readily in the team's work. That pairing could matter for therapy: stress the cell, then remove its shield. The drug's long safety record makes such ideas quicker to test in people. The study adds a mechanism to an old drug's anticancer reputation.
plos-pone-0006504:
Anne-France Petit-Bertron and colleagues studied a histamine receptor in blood formation for PLOS ONE in 2009. The H4 histamine receptor is the most recently characterized of its family. It is expressed preferentially in the bone marrow. That pattern raises the question of its role during hematopoiesis, the making of blood cells.

The authors show that H4 receptors mediate cell cycle arrest in hematopoietic progenitor cells. The effect appears in both murine and human progenitors grown with growth factors. A brake on progenitor division could help balance blood cell production. It also gives histamine, known for allergy, a role in the marrow.
plos-pone-0006604:
Mohammad Fallahi-Sichani and Jennifer Linderman modeled a large family of cell receptors in PLOS ONE in 2009. This family, the G-protein coupled receptors, is the largest set of receptors on cell surfaces. They switch on G-proteins when a signal molecule binds. Many of these receptors work in pairs, and many sit in lipid rafts, which are stiff patches of the cell membrane.

Their model shows how rafts shape receptor signals when the signal molecule changes pairing. Membrane layout can boost or damp a signal in a strong way. Many top drugs act on this receptor family. Knowing raft effects could help make those drugs work in a better and safer way.
plos-pone-0009404:
Anna Torri and co-authors published this immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Dendritic cells are the sentries that show invaders to the rest of the immune system. They can either raise the alarm or calm things down. What gene patterns mark each mood was the team's question.

They isolated RNA from dendritic cells treated with activating or inhibiting substances. Comparing the gene expression profiles revealed inflammatory signatures. Those signatures let researchers read a dendritic cell's state from its genes alone. Such readouts help vaccine and drug designers check whether a treatment wakes the sentries or quiets them.
plos-pone-0009504:
John Mengshol and co-authors studied hepatitis C and liver immune cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. About two hundred million people carry this virus. Most of them stay infected for life, and the liver is slowly harmed. The team focused on galectin-9, a protein that binds sugars. Liver immune cells called Kupffer cells release it.

Galectin-9 from those cells shaped how T cells acted during infection. It could calm some responses and, in context, help the virus persist. The study names this protein as a key lever in the immune fight in the liver. Adjusting it might help patients clear the virus at last.
plos-pone-0009604:
Lasse Ramsgaard and colleagues studied a damage sensing receptor in a mouse model of silicosis in PLOS ONE in 2010. Silicosis scars the lungs of workers who breathe silica dust. No cure exists for the scarring. The receptor, called RAGE, senses signs of tissue damage and can feed inflammation. The team asked what role it plays as the disease develops in mice.

Comparing mice with and without the receptor showed how much of the harm runs through it. If the receptor drives part of the scarring, blocking it could slow the disease. The study tests that logic in a controlled model. It gives a basis for judging RAGE as a treatment target.
plos-pone-0010404:
Elsa Isingrini and colleagues built a mouse model of depression that resists standard drugs, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Depression is common and often disabling, and many patients do not respond to treatment. Research suffers for lack of an animal model of that resistance. The team combined two pressures in mice: repeated mild stress that cannot be predicted, and a high-fat diet. They then tested a standard antidepressant, fluoxetine.

Mice under both pressures responded poorly to the drug. That pairing may mimic patients whose depression comes with metabolic problems. A workable resistance model lets labs screen new treatments that might succeed where old ones fail. It also invites study of how diet and stress interact in the brain. The model is the product here, ready for others to use.
plos-pone-0010504:
Malcolm Leissring and colleagues designed blockers of the enzyme that breaks down insulin in PLOS ONE in 2010. Insulin controls blood sugar, and its loss of control causes diabetes. The body clears insulin mainly by cutting it up with an enzyme called IDE. Blocking that enzyme should, in principle, let insulin act longer. The team designed inhibitors from scratch to fit the enzyme.

Their designed blockers did regulate insulin breakdown and activity in tests. A drug that boosts the body's own insulin could complement existing diabetes care. Design-first approaches show how far structural knowledge has come. The study also warns that IDE handles other proteins, so care is needed. Still, it proves a long-theorized strategy can work in practice.
plos-pone-0010604:
Marko Roblek and colleagues built precision tools for studying diseased lamin proteins, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Lamins form a mesh that supports the cell nucleus. Single-letter changes in lamin A can cause muscle and fat diseases that shorten life.

The team made antibodies that bind only the changed forms, named R453W and R482W. Normal lamin did not attract these antibodies. The tools let researchers spot the faulty protein inside real cells, mixed among healthy copies. Tracking the mutant alone should clarify how one small change damages whole tissues over time.
plos-pone-0010704:
Cecilia Seixas and colleagues tested parts of the cell's folding machine in a pond microbe, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tetrahymena swims and feeds using cilia, tiny beating hairs. Building cilia takes tubulin, a protein that must be folded by a machine called CCT, built from eight different subunits.

Knocking down the CCT alpha or delta subunits crippled cilia growth and upkeep. Cells swam poorly and showed faulty internal structure. Both subunits proved essential, not spare parts. The result ties general protein folding to one clear job, and it gives cilia researchers a clean system for testing folding drugs.
plos-pone-0010804:
Geoffrey Hall and colleagues scanned the brains of adults with autism viewing faint faces, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The amygdala, a small brain hub for emotion, works differently in autism according to many models. Debate remained over whether the difference means weaker or stronger response. Faces shown too briefly to notice offer a clean test of the first, automatic response.

Anxious faces flashed below awareness still engaged the amygdala in autistic adults. The pattern of engagement differed from that of non-autistic adults. Early results of this kind are preliminary by design. They suggest the social brain reacts differently from the very first instant, before thought can intervene.
plos-pone-0010904:
Francis Concepcion and Jeannie Chen published this eye study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Rhodopsin is the light-sensing protein of rod cells in the retina. A human mutation called Q344ter cuts off its tail. That removes the signal that guides it to the right address inside the cell. People with this change slowly lose their vision.

The authors built mice carrying the faulty protein and bred them with mice lacking normal rhodopsin. Dark-raised mutant mice still lost retinal cells, proving that the misplaced protein itself kills photoreceptors. Light made the damage worse, and the stray protein stayed chemically active, switching on signaling partners in the wrong place. Concepcion and Chen show a case where a lost address label turns a working protein toxic, informing research on inherited blindness.
plos-pone-0011004:
Yaqin Xu, Anja Krause, Hiroko Hamai and co-authors published this cystic fibrosis study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The inflamed airways of cystic fibrosis were usually blamed on the defective CFTR channel in airway lining cells. Alveolar macrophages, the lung's resident immune cleaners, also carry CFTR, and the authors asked what happens to them when the channel is silenced.

Turning CFTR down in human macrophages by a hundredfold unleashed an inflammatory phenotype: more IL-8, a potent cell-summoning signal, driven by activation of its master switch, plus more cell death. A membrane protein called caveolin-1 also rose and was investigated as part of the mechanism. Xu and colleagues show the CF lung's inflammation is not only an epithelial problem. Faulty macrophages may fan the very inflammation that destroys CF lungs.
plos-pone-0011104:
Heinisch, Dupres, Wilk and colleagues used a fine imaging tool in PLOS ONE in 2010. With a microscope that can feel single molecules, they looked at a sensor protein in the outer wall of yeast cells. The sensor, called Wsc1, helps yeast detect stress on its surface.

The images showed the sensors gathered in clusters rather than spreading out evenly. Clustering may help the cell sense weak signals and respond as a group. The work shows how surface order shapes cell signaling in a simple organism. Such basic insight often carries over to more complex cells, including human ones.
plos-pone-0011204:
Tsai, Garcia-Gil, Van Haeften and colleagues studied pig sperm in PLOS ONE in 2010. Before a sperm can fertilize an egg, a cap like structure on its head must dock firmly against its outer membrane. The team examined that docking step as sperm become ready inside the female tract.

They showed the docking is stable, holding the cap in place until the right moment. That step is a key part of fertilization that had been hard to pin down. Knowing it informs animal breeding, where sperm quality decides success. It also marks a step that future contraceptive methods could target.
plos-pone-0011304:
Porter, Kelley, George and colleagues found an HIV assembly twist in PLOS ONE in 2010. A protein that normally boosts immune gene reading also interacts with HIV's main building protein. The team tested how this regulator affects the processing of that viral protein inside the cell's main compartment.

The regulator enhanced the cutting and handling of the virus building protein. That moonlighting role could change how much virus a cell produces. It gives HIV research a new host factor to consider as a drug target. Host factors interest drug makers because the virus cannot easily mutate them away.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1304:
Harrison wrote to Stimson again on 17 July 1945, the day Potsdam opened. The acting chairman of the Interim Committee kept the war secretary supplied as the atomic news ripened. Their exchange ran beside the public talks like a second, hidden summit.

Stimson, at Potsdam, was the one man there who carried the whole atomic secret for the American side. Harrison's notes fed him the home end of that file: test word, committee views, and pending choices. This message is one link in that channel. It shows the bomb's policy being handled in quiet notes while the conference made its noise.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1404:
Caffery cabled the acting secretary of state again on 7 August 1945, the day after his cluster of Paris reports. The Potsdam Conference had closed five days earlier. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

The week after a summit is when its choices land on the desks of ambassadors, who must explain them to the governments they live among. Caffery's steady cables show that landing in France. Readers can watch the post-conference work unfold: questions from Paris, answers from the embassy, reports to Washington. It is less grand than the summit itself, and closer to how the settlement was actually carried into the world.
frus-1945-50-intel-d104:
Central Intelligence Group Directive No. 1, dated 19 February 1946, is the new body's first numbered order. The CIG had been created by the president's directive four weeks earlier. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

First directives set a body's working habits: who may task it, what it may collect, and how its products reach the departments. Directive No. 1 turned the January compromise into daily practice. Readers should read it as the CIG's birth certificate in operational form. Everything the group later became, a true central agency in embryo, starts from the authorities and limits written here, under its first director, Sidney Souers.
frus-1945-50-intel-d204:
A memorandum dated 23 January 1947 links two senior offices. The sender was the Chief of the Legislative Liaison Division of the Central Intelligence Group (Pforzheimer). The reader was the Director of Central Intelligence (Vandenberg). Readers meet it as document 204 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The postwar system was still new: the National Intelligence Authority gave the orders, and the Central Intelligence Group carried them out.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. The note's brevity hides its weight: men at this level did not write to each other for practice. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d304:
A letter from Secretary of Defense Forrestal reached Acting Secretary of State Lovett on 13 October 1948. It is document 304 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. An outside survey team led by Allen Dulles was then reviewing the CIA, and its findings would drive a round of reform debate.

A letter fixed a position in a way a phone call never could: dated, signed, and filed for both sides to cite later. Its worth now is the voice: a chief stating his case as he wished it to be read. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d404:
James Lay, acting executive secretary of the National Security Council, sent a memo to the Council itself on 14 December 1949. The paper is document 404 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The Council joined the President with his top foreign and defense aides. Its executive secretary handled the flow of papers that set up each meeting and recorded each choice. A memo from that office to the Council shows the staff machine behind Cold War choices at the highest level. Lay later held the secretary's post in full, a sign of the trust this staff work earned.
frus-1861-d104:
Lord Lyons wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 28 October 1861. The letter is document 104 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Lyons's last October note in the file keeps the formal round intact. The two governments had learned to argue without breaking. That habit, built letter by letter, would soon be tested harder than either man yet knew. That habit of formal calm would soon face the Trent, the hardest test of the war's first year. The hardest test found the habit strong, which is why the tie survived it.
frus-1861-d204:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Eduard de Stoeckl on 7 September 1861. De Stoeckl was the Russian minister in Washington. The letter is document 204 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

De Stoeckl had served in Washington for years and knew its ways well. Seward's letter to him worked the home end of the Russian tie. Between them, the two men kept the warmest link the Union had in Europe running smoothly. De Stoeckl's long service made him half an insider in the capital he served. Half an insider is a rare post for a foreign envoy, and he filled it well.
frus-1861-d304:
Seward's incoming mail for 27 July 1861 held a dispatch from Mr. Turpin. The printed record keeps it as Document 304 in the President's message volume for 1861. The letter comes from the first summer of the Civil War, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d104:
17 July 1862 is the date on a dispatch from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London to William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 104 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. By then, in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d204:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons on 13 January 1862, in a note printed as Document 204 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, handled the American war from the legation there.

Mid-January found both governments glad to leave the Trent quarrel behind, yet watchful. The Union blockade of Southern ports and British trade losses from it promised fresh disputes. Short formal notes like this one were the everyday tools for managing those disputes before they hardened, and the file holds many from this winter. Formal notes left a paper record that both governments could quote back to each other later.
frus-1862-d304:
Dated 18 August 1862, Document 304 is a dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward to William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris. It is printed in the France section of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

The letter went out eleven days before the second battle of Bull Run, in the last stretch of the summer's buildup. Seward's tone in this period stayed formal and assured, whatever the news. That practiced calm was policy: envoys abroad took their cue from the Secretary's voice, and foreign governments read it as a measure of Union confidence. Seward paired Dayton's reports with Mercier's remarks in Washington to test each against the other.
frus-1862-d404:
One day after his previous order, on 24 June 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote once more to Horace J. Perry in Madrid. The note is Document 404 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress with the annual message.

Back-to-back instructions usually meant fast-moving news or a point Seward wanted stressed without delay. In June 1862 the fighting in Virginia and the allied quarrel in Mexico both pressed on Spanish policy. Small as it is, the dispatch shows how closely Washington managed its Madrid post. Much of Civil War diplomacy was done this way, in brief, frequent letters rather than grand notes.
frus-1862-d504:
On 4 June 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to James Shepherd Pike at The Hague. It is Document 504 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

June opened with the armies facing each other before Richmond and the war's outcome once again in doubt. Seward's orders that month mixed resolve with careful answers to specific Dutch questions about ports and shipping. The Netherlands file in the volume is long because both sides wrote often and on small matters as well as large. An instruction of this kind is best read as maintenance: keeping a friendly neutrality in good repair while the great battles were decided elsewhere.
frus-1862-d604:
Admiral Jurien de la Gravière, the French naval commander in the Mexican expedition, wrote this letter to Spain's General Prim on 20 March 1862. It is Document 604 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, annexed to Prim's own despatch.

An annex travels with the document that encloses it. So a French admiral's letter survives here inside a Spanish general's report. The report is printed in an American volume. The layering is the point: the allied commanders in Mexico were already at odds that March, and their private exchanges show it. For the reader, the letter is a small, sharp piece of the coalition's breakup, preserved through three governments' paperwork.
frus-1862-d704:
Charles N. Riotte sent this dispatch from Costa Rica to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 14 September 1862. Riotte was the American minister there. The letter is document 704 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

By the fall of 1862 Riotte had a year's worth of Central American ground to report on. His mail dealt with the republics' affairs, the transit trade, and the claims of Americans in the region. Letters like this one formed Washington's best source on a part of the world it cared about chiefly for the road between the seas. The record still shows that care, one dispatch at a time.
frus-1863p1-d104:
On 2 March 1863, William H. Seward wrote this letter to Charles Francis Adams, the eighth of twelve to him dated that day in the volume. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 104 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Late in a long batch, a writer turns to the smaller heads of a brief: the points that need a word but not a speech. Seward's eighth sheet of the day is of that kind, by its place in the row. Together the twelve gave Adams a full kit for the spring's talks in London. This letter is one tool in that kit, plain and to its point.
frus-1863p1-d204:
To guide his minister in London, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote these orders on 19 May 1863 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. They stand as document 204 of the 1863 volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Orders crossed the Atlantic by steamship and took ten days or more to arrive. By the time Adams acted, events in London could already have moved on. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d304:
The Secretary of State, William H. Seward, wrote to his minister in London, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, on 5 October 1863. The letter is document 304 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Adams was told to deal chiefly with Lord John Russell, the foreign secretary. Seward's letters armed him with facts and wording for those meetings. By then the British government had moved to hold the Confederate rams, and the sharpest crisis of the year was cooling. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d404: On 28 February 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 404 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, part of the formal exchange through which the two governments handled Civil War disputes. Notes on this route dealt with neutral rights, stopped ships, and British complaints.
frus-1863p1-d504:
Secretary William H. Seward directed a letter to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons on 11 May 1863. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d604:
Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons took up his pen on 7 August 1863 and wrote to William H. Seward, Secretary of State. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the late summer of 1863.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
plos-pbio-0020004:
Tomoko Ishino, Kazuhiko Yano, Yasuo Chinzei, and their group traced a step in malaria infection for PLOS Biology in 2004. After a mosquito bite, malaria parasites travel to the liver. A sheet of cells lines the liver's blood vessels, and the parasites must cross it to reach liver cells.

The team found that the parasites need a cell-passage skill to make that crossing. They actively move through cells rather than slipping between them. Blocking that skill could, in theory, stop infection before the liver stage takes hold. The paper matters because the liver stage is a brief, quiet window. A drug or vaccine that works there could prevent illness outright.
plos-pbio-0020104:
Zhixin Xie, Lisa K. Johansen, Adam M. Gustafson, and a large team mapped small RNA pathways in plants for PLOS Biology in 2004. Plants use small RNAs to silence genes, fight viruses, and control growth. The team sorted the many small RNAs of the model plant Arabidopsis and traced how they are made.

They found that the pathways branch more than expected, with distinct sets of small RNAs doing distinct jobs. Some guard the genome against jumping genes, while others fine-tune growth genes. A full catalog of these RNAs gives plant science a working map. It also informs crop work, since the same pathways shape traits like yield and disease resistance.
plos-pbio-0020304:
Dennis R. Harris, Masashi Tanaka, Sergei V. Saveliev, and their team studied a radiation-proof bacterium in PLOS Biology in 2004. Deinococcus radiodurans survives doses of radiation that shatter its genome into hundreds of pieces, then rebuilds it. The authors focus on a protein called DdrA that appears after damage.

DdrA guards the broken ends of DNA, keeping them from being chewed away before repair starts. That protection buys time for the cell's rebuilding tools. The bacterium's tricks are of keen interest for cleaning up radioactive waste and for understanding DNA repair in general. Each named part, like DdrA, brings the full system closer to view.
plos-pone-0000104:
Michael A. Pickart, Eric W. Klee, Aubrey L. Nielsen, and a large team built a genetics toolkit in PLOS ONE in 2006. The secretome is the set of proteins a cell secretes, its outward messages and tools. Many of their jobs were unknown. The team's framework knocks down these genes one by one in vertebrate embryos to reveal their roles.

Reverse genetics starts from the gene and asks what breaks without it. Applied at genome scale to secreted proteins, it promises a catalog of what our cells say to each other. Secreted proteins are prime drug targets, since they can be reached outside the cell. A map of their functions is thus both basic biology and a drug hunter's chart.
plos-pone-0000204:
Nikolas Nikolaidis, Dimitra Chalkia, D. Neil Watkins, and colleagues published this evolution paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It argues for the ancient origin of a group of developmental genes the authors call DANGER, described as a new developmental superfamily. These genes are involved in how embryos build their bodies.

Tracing a gene family to an ancient origin changes when scientists think its roles began. The authors compare sequences across species to date the family. If the superfamily is as old as they argue, its genes were part of the toolkit of very early animals, not a later addition.
plos-pone-0000304:
Xavier Dramard, Thierry Heidmann, and Silke Jensen published this genetics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. The I-factor is a LINE retrotransposon, a jumping gene in fruit flies that can cause sterility when it runs loose. The authors describe natural epigenetic protection against it: fragments left by ancestral invasions of the element silence the modern copies.

The genome, in effect, keeps souvenirs of old invasions that vaccinate it against new ones. The authors document that protection in Drosophila. The work is a neat case of an arms race written into DNA, where the host's defense is built from the invader's own remains.
plos-pone-0000404:
Remus Oşan and colleagues applied a mathematical technique to brain data in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Neural networks in the brain encode information in patterns spread across many cells, and those patterns are hard to read from raw recordings. The team used subspace projection methods to classify and display these network-level encoding patterns.

Subspace projection simplifies high-dimensional data by finding the directions that carry the real signal. Applied to neural activity, it can sort patterns by what they represent and show them in pictures a human can grasp. Better readouts of population activity serve research on memory, movement, and brain-computer interfaces, where decoding many cells at once is the whole problem.
plos-pone-0000504:
Cindy Voisine and colleagues used a millimeter-long worm to screen for Huntington's disease drugs, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Huntington's is a fatal inherited brain disease with no cure. The worm Caenorhabditis elegans can be engineered to carry the disease's defect, and the team used it for identification of potential therapeutic drugs.

Worms are cheap, fast, and easy to dose, so thousands of compounds can be tested in weeks. Hits from a worm screen still face a long road through mouse and human testing, but the screen widens the funnel's mouth. The study is an example of model-organism drug discovery aimed at a disease that human trials alone cannot explore quickly.
plos-pone-0000604:
Elena M. Boggio and colleagues watched a signaling enzyme light up in two cell compartments at once after visual input, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. ERK is an enzyme that relays activity signals inside neurons. The team showed that visual stimulation activates ERK in two parts of rat cortical neurons. ERK rose in the synaptic compartment and in the somatic compartment. Both responses ran on the same timetable.

Parallel timing suggests the synapse and the nucleus-bound machinery are coordinated when the visual system adapts to input. ERK activation is a step in plasticity, the process by which seeing reshapes the seeing brain. Rat visual cortex is a standard model for how experience tunes sensory systems early in life.
plos-pone-0000704:
Jeroen R. P. M. Strating, Gerrit Bouw, Theo G. M. Hafmans and colleagues compared two members of a protein transport family, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The p24 family is thought to help move proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi, the cell's shipping and sorting stations. A subset of p24 proteins rises when frog pituitary cells are activated to produce more hormone.

The title previews a contrast: p24 alpha and p24 delta have disparate effects on secretory protein transport and processing. Two relatives pulling differently complicates any simple family story. For cell biologists, sorting out who does what in the early secretory pathway underpins everything cells export, from hormones to antibodies.
plos-pone-0000804:
Tsunglin Liu, Thales Papagiannakopoulos, Kathy Puskar and colleagues searched living tissue data for the fingerprint of microRNAs, in PLOS ONE in 2007. MicroRNAs are short non-coding transcripts, about 21 nucleotides long, capable of regulating gene expression. The best-studied mechanism has a microRNA binding its target messenger RNA, after which translation is inhibited and the message may be destroyed.

If microRNAs act in vivo, sets of real mRNAs should carry a detectable signal of that action, in their sequences or levels. The team reports detecting such a signal in an in vivo expression set. Confirming lab mechanisms in whole organisms tells researchers microRNA rules learned in dishes still govern living systems.
plos-pone-0000904:
Eriikka Heikkinen, Teemu Kallonen, Lilli Saarinen and colleagues compared whooping cough germs across Finland, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Bordetella pertussis causes whooping cough and has returned in many countries. Finland has used the whole cell vaccine for more than fifty years, yet cases rose again.

The team compared genomes of Finnish strains and report steady gene loss over time. A germ that sheds genes while a vaccine presses on it raises hard questions about adaptation. Their comparison helps health officials judge whether vaccines still match the germ in circulation. It also shows evolution at work inside a single country.
plos-pone-0001004:
Samantha Morris, Alexandra Almeida, Hideaki Tanaka and colleagues showed how a factor called Tsukushi tunes embryo signals, in PLOS ONE in 2007. In early frog development, the middle germ layer forms when lower cells signal to cells above them. Whole body layers arise from such local conversations.

Tsukushi modulates three signal families at once: Xnr2, FGF and BMP. Tuning several signals together can set the borders of the germ layers with precision. The work was done in Xenopus, the standard frog for embryo studies. A single factor touching three pathways is a reminder that embryo signals form a web, not separate wires.
plos-pone-0001104:
Jeffrey Petrella, Steven Prince, Lihong Wang and colleagues tested a brain signal's power to predict decline in mild cognitive impairment, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Healthy people deactivate a region called the posteromedial cortex during many tasks. Brain imaging had suggested that this deactivation during memory tasks is impaired in Alzheimer's disease.

Mild cognitive impairment sits between normal aging and Alzheimer's. The team assess the prognostic value of posteromedial deactivation in such patients: does a weaker signal foresee worse decline. A predictor at this stage would help families plan and trials recruit the right patients. Imaging markers are plentiful; prognostic proof is the rare part.
plos-pone-0001204:
When immune cells meet, they form a structured contact zone called the immunological synapse. Oded Rechavi and colleagues report a surprising event at that zone in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. An oncogenic protein, H-Ras, transfers from one cell to another there. The synapse is known for regions of membrane fusion and exchanges of membrane fragments between the cells.

The authors show that the cancer-associated form of H-Ras moves between cells at the synapse. A growth-promoting protein passing hand to hand could change how the receiving cell behaves. The finding adds a new route by which signals, healthy or harmful, spread through the immune system.
plos-pone-0001304:
Scrapie is a fatal brain disease of sheep caused by prions, infectious proteins. Gillian McGovern and Martin Jeffrey describe the disease's specific pathology in sheep lymphoid tissues, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Prion diseases often cause accumulation of the disease-associated prion protein in the lymphoreticular system, the network of immune tissues.

The protein builds up in association with follicular dendritic cells and tingible body macrophages in secondary lymphoid organs. Mapping exactly where it accumulates helps diagnose scrapie from tissue samples, which matters for flock surveillance. The lymphoid pattern also hints at how prions spread through the body before reaching the brain.
plos-pone-0001404:
Sheena Lee and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on spinal muscular atrophy, a gene based ill that weakens muscle. In this disease, one gene is lost, but a near twin gene gives weak backup. The protein's full job was still not clear. The team read gene use across the genome in a model of the disease.

Their broad scan named sets of genes whose use shifts when the key protein is low. Those shifts point to paths that may drive the muscle loss. They also give a list of fresh drug targets to test. The work moves from one lost gene to the wider web it disturbs.
plos-pone-0001504:
Mehmet Somel and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on diet and gene use in humans and chimps. The human diet strays far from that of our close primate kin. What that stray means for gene gaps was unknown. The team fed lab mice diets in the style of human or chimp food.

Gene use in the mice shifted with diet. Some shifts copied the known gaps between human and chimp gene use. That hints diet alone can drive part of the species gap. It warns that gene comparisons must weigh food and lab life. It also gives a tool to test diet effects in a strict way.
plos-pone-0001604:
Dean Smith, Julie Rosenheimer, and Ronald Kalil published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on ion channels in young rat nerve stem cells. These channels help set how cells fire, and they matter for growth and cell division. No full account of them existed for nerve stem cells from the rat brain's growth zone. The team recorded the currents cell by cell.

They chart two main channel types and how each opens and shuts. The chart is a base map for how these stem cells talk in bursts. It helps labs tell stem cells from their mature kin by their currents. It may also hint at how channel faults skew brain growth.
plos-pone-0001704:
Geraldine A. Wright, Sonya M. Kottcamp, and Mitchell G. A. Thomson studied how honeybees judge odors in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Animals use smells to tell mates, kin, and food apart, even though natural odor amounts vary a lot. Generalization, treating two different stimuli as alike, helps an animal decide that a changed smell still means the same thing.

The authors show that generalization is what lets bees stay sensitive to complex odor features despite that variation. The full text gives the training tests, the odor blends, and the bees' choices. The work explains a puzzle in animal senses. A nose can be both finely tuned and tolerant of noise, a balance that robot sensors still struggle to copy.
plos-pone-0001804:
Mustafa Raoof, Haq Nawaz, Rabeeya Nusrat, and their co-authors surveyed sedative use in Pakistan in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Benzodiazepines are prescribed too freely in Pakistan and are available over the counter without prescription, a major public health problem. Data on how much people knew about these drugs, and how much they used them, was limited.

Their one-time survey covered healthy volunteers and clinic patients visiting a large care hospital. The full text gives how much people knew, the usage rates, and where people got the drugs. Benzodiazepines are habit forming, so measuring casual use and low awareness gives health chiefs the baseline they need to tighten supply and warn the public.
plos-pone-0001904:
Wassim Chehab and co-authors split apart two plant defense signals in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. When pests or germs attack, plants fire back with chemical defenses. Two groups of signals drive much of that response. One is the jasmonates, and the other is six-carbon aldehydes, both made from fats in the leaf by two rival branches of one pathway.

Because the branches compete, their roles are hard to untangle. The team used plants in which one branch or the other was changed, to see what each signal group does on its own. Clear roles for each signal help crop science breed or treat plants that resist pests with fewer sprays.
plos-pone-0002004:
Elizabeth Clement and co-authors recorded brain waves that cycle like sleep under anesthesia, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Sleep and general anesthesia both bring unconsciousness and share some brain steps. But sleep is not flat: it cycles between active REM sleep and quiet sleep. Whether anesthesia shows like cycles was less clear.

Under urethane anesthesia, a standard lab drug, the team recorded spontaneous shifts of brain state. As the title states, the brain showed cyclic, sleep-like alternations. If an anesthetized brain still cycles, depth of anesthesia may rise and fall on its own. That fact matters for both brain science and surgery.
plos-pone-0002104:
Timur Akchurin and co-authors tracked the birth and death of bone-eating cells in long-term culture, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Osteoclasts are the cells that resorb bone. They contribute to degenerative, metabolic, and neoplastic bone diseases, which often show lasting changes in the bone's local setting. How a population of these cells rises and falls over time was not well charted.

The team aimed to investigate the dynamics of osteoclast formation and death in cultures kept for the long term. They report complex dynamics, not a simple rise and fade. Bone drugs act on these very dynamics.
plos-pone-0002204:
Kwasi Torpey, Mushota Kabaso, Liya Mutale, and co-authors described a staffing fix for HIV care in Zambia, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Clinics offering antiretroviral therapy, the drugs that keep HIV in check, face severe staff shortages. Good adherence counseling helps patients take their drugs on schedule, but nurses and doctors have little time for it.

The Zambia Prevention, Care and Treatment Partnership trained community volunteers as adherence support workers at health facilities. These lay workers took on counseling and follow-up tasks. The program shows how care can be shared more widely, so scarce clinical staff can focus on the work only they can do.
plos-pone-0002304:
Heather Ishak, John Dumbacher, Nancy Anderson, and co-authors surveyed blood parasites in owls, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. All three subspecies of the Spotted Owl are threatened by habitat loss and by the spread of the Barred Owl into their range. One unexamined threat was whether Barred Owls carry blood parasites that could infect Spotted Owls.

The team screened owls for blood parasites and compared what each species carries. If the invading Barred Owl brings new parasites, contact between the two could add disease pressure to a bird already losing ground. Surveys like this one tell conservation teams whether disease belongs on the threat list.
plos-pone-0002404:
Led by Iwai, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Yoshiko Iwai, Hiroaki Hemmi, Olga Mizenina, and others. Its subject is an IFN-γ-IL-18 Signaling Loop Accelerates Memory CD8 + T Cell Proliferation. Rapid proliferation is one of the important features of memory CD8 + T cells, ensuring rapid clearance of reinfection.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002504:
Research by Hemminki and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Kari Hemminki, Asta Försti, Justo Lorenzo Bermejo, and others. Its subject is the ‘Common Disease-Common Variant’ Hypothesis and Familial Risks. The recent large genotyping studies have identified a new repertoire of disease susceptibility loci of unknown function.

Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002604:
Bunnell and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Tina M. Bunnell, Michele A. Jaeger, Daniel P. Fitzsimons, and others. Its subject is destabilization of the Dystrophin-Glycoprotein Complex without Functional Deficits in α-Dystrobrevin Null Muscle. α-Dystrobrevin is a component of the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex (DGC) and is thought to have both structural and signaling roles in skeletal muscle.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002704:
Research from Eva Madi Riising and co-authors, published in PLOS ONE in 2008, covers the polycomb repressive complex 2 is a potential target of SUMO modifications. The catalog record names Eva Madi Riising first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. The Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) functions as a transcriptional repressor through a mechanism that involves methylation of Histone H3 at lysine 27. The authors add a further point. The PRC2 complex activity is essential for cellular proliferation, development, and cell fate decisions. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002804:
Work by Sigeng Chen and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008, dealing with dopamine inhibits mitochondrial motility in hippocampal neurons. Authorship is credited in the record to Sigeng Chen and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. The trafficking of mitochondria within neurons is a highly regulated process. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002904:
Jijun Hao, Marie Daleo, Clare Murphy and co-authors tested a small drug called dorsomorphin in stem cells in 2008. Embryonic stem cells can become any tissue type, which makes them a hopeful source for repair medicine. Guiding them into one chosen type, such as heart muscle, needs precise signals.

Dorsomorphin selectively blocks BMP signaling, one of those growth signals. In PLOS ONE the team reports that blocking BMP this way promotes cardiomyogenesis, the making of heart muscle cells, in embryonic stem cells. That gives labs a simple chemical tool for steering stem cells toward the heart.
plos-pone-0003004:
Sven Hoffmann and Michael Falkenstein compared two ways to clean eye blink artifacts from EEG in 2008. Blinks swamp the brain signals that electroencephalograms record. The study investigated what impact blinks leave behind after correction by a regression method and by independent component analysis.

The two prominent methods are named EMCP for the regression approach and ICA for the component approach. Published in PLOS ONE, a head-to-head check on residual impact helps labs pick a cleaning method with evidence. Clean EEG matters for any study reading thought or perception from scalp signals. The complete article sets out the methods and data behind each claim in full.
plos-pone-0003104:
Adam de Smith, Robin Walters, Lachlan Coin and co-authors studied small deletion variants in human DNA in 2008. Copy number variants contribute greatly to human genomic variation, with over 5,000 loci reported covering more than 18 percent of the genome. Little was known about the origin and stability of variants of different sizes.

Small deletions have stable breakpoints commonly associated with Alu elements, repeated DNA sequences, the title reports. Stable break points suggest these variants arise and persist in orderly ways. Published in PLOS ONE, the work helps interpret the deletions found in patient genome scans.
plos-pone-0003204:
Monika Madan and Salomon Amar link an immune sensor to atherosclerosis in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Accumulating evidence implicates a fundamental link between the immune system and atherosclerosis, the artery disease behind most heart attacks. Toll-like receptors are principal sensors of the innate immune system. The team report an assessment of the role of the TLR2 pathway in atherosclerosis linked with a high-fat diet and pathogens.

They present proteomic findings, a broad survey of proteins, to support that role. Readers see diet, infection and immunity drawn into one artery story. The work suggests immune sensors could be targets in heart disease prevention.
plos-pone-0003304:
Bindu Chandrasekharan, Vanitha Bala, Vasantha L. Kolachala and colleagues delete a neuropeptide gene in a colitis model in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Neurogenic inflammation plays a major role in the pathogenesis of inflammatory bowel disease. The team examined the role of neuropeptide Y and neuronal nitric oxide synthase in shaping colitis. Colitis was induced by giving dextran sodium sulphate.

The title reports that targeted deletion of neuropeptide Y modulates experimental colitis. Readers see gut nerves treated as active players in bowel inflammation, not bystanders. Nerve signals may offer drug angles apart from calming the immune system alone.
plos-pone-0007404:
Stephen J. Lycett used stone tools to trace ancient hominin dispersals in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Reconstructing dispersal patterns of extinct hominins is challenging but essential. Archaeological evidence in the form of stone tools can supplement the sparse fossil record, because tools survive far more often than bones in most ancient sites.

Acheulean handaxes spread widely across the Old World. Based on broad dating, their appearance marked major population movements. Lycett performs a phylogeographic analysis of handaxe data, treating tool variation like inherited traits. His approach tests whether handaxe patterns match proposed dispersal routes out of Africa.
plos-pone-0007504:
Isabelle-Anne Bisson, Kamran Safi, and Richard Holland published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how migration evolved in bats. More than thirty bat species migrate, some over long distances. Bird migration has been studied for decades, but bat migration drew little notice. The team looked at the largest bat family and traced migration on its family tree. They asked whether the habit arose once or many times.

The evidence points to repeated, separate origins of migration. Distinct branches of the family invented the traveling life on their own. Such repeat invention hints that the pressures favoring migration are strong and common. It also lets scientists compare branch by branch to find what triggers the habit. The study brings a neglected group into a classic question. Its answer favors many origins over a single one.
plos-pone-0007604:
Ikjin Kim and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the cell's protein quality control. Misfolded proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum are eliminated by a pathway called ER-associated degradation. Failure of that disposal underlies many diseases, including neurodegenerative ones. A protein called Usa1 helps the pathway tag targets with ubiquitin, the cell's disposal label. The team dissected how Usa1 does its helping.

Usa1 facilitates the tagging through two separate domains. Each domain contributes its own part to substrate ubiquitylation. A helper with two hands can hold the machinery and the target together. Understanding such helpers clarifies how the disposal system chooses its victims. That system protects every cell that makes secreted proteins. The study adds fine detail to a pathway whose breakdown is costly.
plos-pone-0007704:
Nadege Sarrazin and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It concerns receptors for stress hormones in a brain area called the dentate gyrus. These glucocorticoid receptors switch genes on and off in brain cells. High hormone levels acting through them can shift behavior.

The team changed receptor activity in that one brain region in mice. The change altered which genes were switched on there. It also raised anxiety-related behavior in the animals. The results tie a single brain circuit to stress and anxiety, and point to a target for future treatments.
plos-pone-0007804:
George Han and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tests tiny particles that release nitric oxide against a stubborn germ. Staphylococcus aureus is a leading cause of skin abscesses and other infections. Nitric oxide is part of the body's natural defense against it.

Using the gas as a drug had been limited by delivery problems. The team packed it into nanoparticles that let it out slowly. In a mouse model, the particles treated abscesses caused by the germ. A topical particle therapy could add a weapon against drug-resistant staph infections.
plos-pone-0007904:
Luisa Cironi and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It explains why one cancer-causing fusion protein works in some cells but not others. Nearly all synovial sarcomas carry a fusion gene, SYT-SSX1, born from a chromosome swap. The tumor is thought to start in primitive stem cells.

The authors tested human mesenchymal stem cells, a candidate cell of origin. Their epigenetic features decided whether the cells were permissive. Only in the right epigenetic state did SYT-SSX1 switch on its target genes. The work shows a cancer gene needs a receptive cell to act.
plos-pone-0008004:
Takayuki Manabe and colleagues cataloged where a DNA-bending protein likes to land in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein, HMGA1a, shapes DNA to help switch genes on and off. It favors stretches rich in the letters A and T.

The team gathered candidate landing spots across the human genome. Each spot is a place where this shaping hand may do its work, from growth to immune defense. The catalog turns a vague sense of the protein's reach into a map that other teams can test gene by gene. Each entry on the list can now be checked in focused lab tests.
plos-pone-0008104:
Iris Alchanati and colleagues found the crew that clears a poisoned DNA enzyme in PLOS ONE in 2009. Some cancer drugs work by trapping topoisomerase enzymes on DNA, where they block and break the strand. The cell must clear those traps for the drug to kill cleanly.

A tagging enzyme pair, Bmi1 and Ring1A, marks the trapped Top2 alpha for the cell's shredder. Without the marks, the traps linger. The clearing path is a fresh drug target: blocking it might make standard cancer drugs bite harder at lower doses. The pair now joins the short list of known clearing crews.
plos-pone-0008204:
Till Geib and Klemens J. Hertel reported a gene therapy approach in PLOS ONE in 2009 for spinal muscular atrophy. The disease is inherited and destroys motor neurons, the cells that drive muscle. It stems from loss or faults of the SMN1 gene. A backup copy, SMN2, remains but makes only low levels of the needed protein.

The team used adenoviral vectors to deliver antisense pieces built into U7 small RNAs. These pieces push SMN2 to make full-length SMN protein. Raising protein from the backup gene could ease the disease. The work tests one route toward treatment for affected children.
plos-pone-0008304:
Francisca Gushiken and her team wrote in PLOS ONE in 2009 about how blood clots form in mice. A clot starts when a part on the platelet surface, called an integrin, is switched on. Platelets are the small blood cells that seal cuts. Kinase and phosphatase proteins inside the platelet run the switch. One phosphatase part, PP1c gamma, was their main focus.

They tested how this part shapes the platelet response to thrombin. Thrombin is a strong clot signal found in blood. The switch must be firm but not too firm, or clots may block a vein. Their work shows, step by step, how one small part helps set that balance.
plos-pone-0008404:
Bridget A. Quinn and colleagues created a mouse model of ovarian cancer in PLOS ONE in 2009. About one in ten epithelial ovarian cancers is inherited. Most inherited cases result from mutations in the BRCA1 gene. Mutations in p53 are also often found in these cancers. The team conditionally inactivated both genes in mouse ovaries.

Turning off Brca1 and p53 induced ovarian leiomyosarcomas in the mice. These are cancers of smooth muscle tissue in the ovary. A model that produces tumors on demand helps test treatments. It also shows how two famous cancer genes cooperate.
plos-pone-0008504:
Edward Cachay and co-authors study hidden infections in HIV-positive men in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Health guidance recommends screening for sexually transmitted infections in such men. The guidance rests on self-report of unprotected anal sex. But some men deny risk behavior when asked. The team ask if denial rules out silent anorectal infection. Silent cases show no symptoms yet can harm health and spread.

They test men regardless of what they reported. They estimate how valid self-report is for screening decisions. Denial does not exclude asymptomatic infection in their data. Screening rules based only on self-report would miss real cases.
plos-pone-0008604:
Anatasha Crawford and co-authors study drug resistance in breast cancer in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. BCL2 family members affect cell fate decisions in breast cancer. The role of BCL-W, also called BCL2L2, was unknown. Both BCL-W and BCL2 block apoptosis, the cell death program. Antiestrogen drugs such as fulvestrant treat hormone-sensitive breast cancers. The team test how these blockers affect response to that drug, using cell and tumor models.

Co-inhibition of BCL-W and BCL2 restores antiestrogen sensitivity. It does so through BECN1, a gene that drives autophagy. The treated cells die by an autophagy-associated necrosis. Blocking both survival proteins may rescue failing hormone therapy.
plos-pone-0008704:
Mutsuki Amano, Yuta Tsumura, Kentaro Taki, and colleagues built a dragnet for kinase targets. Their methods study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Kinases are enzymes that tag other proteins with phosphate groups. Each tag can switch a protein on or off. Mapping which proteins a kinase tags reveals whole signaling routes. Such mapping is slow when done one protein at a time.

Their protein-chip approach screens many candidate proteins in parallel. They tested it on Rho-kinase, a kinase that shapes cell movement and tension. The screen caught known targets and flagged new ones. Other kinase studies can borrow the same broad net.
plos-pone-0008804:
Sharon Perry, Bouke de Jong, Jay Solnick, and colleagues reported a surprising shield against tuberculosis. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Helicobacter pylori lives in the stomach for life, usually without symptoms. It reshapes stomach immunity in lasting ways. Such reshaping might spill over to other infections. Tuberculosis, a slow lung germ, was the test case.

People carrying H. pylori showed signs of protection against tuberculosis. The stomach germ may keep certain defenses on alert. A usually unwelcome resident could thus do quiet good. The finding complicates plans to wipe out H. pylori everywhere.
plos-pone-0008904:
Stuart Meier, Oziniel Ruzvidzo, Monique Morse, and colleagues gave a plant defense gene a second job as a signal maker. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Plants link outside warnings to responses using messenger chemicals. One messenger, cGMP, serves in many plant processes. The Arabidopsis gene WAKL10 sits in the cell wall's sensing system. Its activity rose alongside known pathogen defense genes, hinting at an immune role.

Tests showed the WAKL10 protein truly makes cGMP, acting as a guanylyl cyclase. A wall sensor that also brews a messenger tightens the alarm chain. Plant immunity gains a new named link between attack and response.
plos-pone-0009004:
Michael Siegal and co-authors asked whether growing up with two languages sharpens children's social sense, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bilingual children are common worldwide, but their conversational skills were little studied. Understanding talk means catching irony, white lies, and what speakers really mean. The study involved children aged three to six.

The children were exposed to English, German, Italian, Japanese, or pairs of those languages. Bilingual children read the point of conversations better than one-language children. Juggling two tongues seems to train attention to a speaker's intent. The edge adds a social benefit to the known list for bilingual upbringing.
plos-pone-0009104:
Lina Shehadeh and co-authors proposed a blood marker that might expose Parkinson's disease early, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Roughly five million people around the world live with Parkinson's, a slow brain disease. Diagnosis still rests on a doctor reading symptoms and patterns of movement. No lab test could yet confirm the disease or catch it beforehand.

The team screened patients' blood for signs of heavy alternative splicing. One gene, SRRM2, stood out clearly in the blood samples from patients. SRRM2 itself helps run the cell's splicing machinery day to day. A blood flag like this could sharpen diagnosis and open detection before symptoms show.
plos-pone-0009204:
Loro Kujjo and colleagues published this fertility study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cancer treatment often damages a woman's eggs, and current ways to save her fertility work poorly. The same loss happens with plain aging. The team looked for the switches that decide whether a damaged egg repairs itself or dies.

Working with mouse egg cells, they targeted two proteins, Bax and Rad51. Bax helps push damaged cells toward death, while Rad51 helps repair broken DNA. Adjusting those targets raised the survival of eggs after chemotherapy or aging. The result points toward treatments that could protect fertility instead of only trying to replace lost eggs.
plos-pone-0009304:
Hans-Christian Ingerslev and co-authors published this fish immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fibroblasts are the cells that build connective tissue and repair wounds. In mammals they also act as immune sentinels, sounding alarms when tissue is damaged. Almost nothing was known about that role in fish.

The team worked with a fibroblast cell line from rainbow trout skin. The cells responded to signals from germs and from damaged tissue alike. They switched on genes tied to immune defense. The result says fish fibroblasts are front-line watchers too, not just builders, which changes how fish immunity is pictured.
plos-pone-0011404:
Tokuhiro Chano and colleagues showed in 2010 that a protein called RB1CC1 can switch a key growth brake back on in human cancer cells. The RB1 pathway normally stops cells from dividing without control, and cancers often disable it. Rather than adding a foreign drug, the team raised the level of this built-in activator.

With more RB1CC1, cancer cells grew more slowly and formed far fewer colonies, the lab sign of a tumor's power to spread from single cells. Reactivating a brake the cell already owns is an appealing strategy, since it works with normal control systems. The result names RB1CC1 as both a marker and a possible lever in cancer. Tumors that have lost it may be the ones most in need of drugs that restore the same braking effect.
plos-pone-0011504:
Federico Calboli and co-authors ran a genome-wide association study in 2010 hunting genes behind neuroticism. The trait, a tendency toward worry and emotional volatility, runs in families and predicts anxiety and depression, yet its genetic roots had stayed elusive. The team scanned DNA variants across the genome in a population-based sample and tested each for a link to the trait.

A genome-wide scan is a disciplined kind of hunt: it makes no guesses about which genes matter and corrects strictly for the huge number of tests. Whatever survives that discipline is a lead the field can trust and follow. Personality genetics needs such hard data, since candidate-gene stories in psychology have often failed to replicate. The study adds a firm, population-level footing to one of psychology's most studied traits.
plos-pone-0011604:
Kai Tang and colleagues rebuilt the family tree of Roseobacter bacteria from whole genomes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Roseobacters live in ocean surface waters worldwide and can make up a large share of all bacteria there. They help drive the ocean's chemical cycles, moving carbon and other elements through sea life.

With many new genome sequences in hand, the team compared them to chart how this group diversified. Their tree shows lineages spreading into varied roles across coastal and open waters. Understanding that split helps scientists predict how these abundant microbes respond as oceans warm and change.
plos-pone-0011704:
Bradley Schneider and co-authors looked at how mosquito spit shapes West Nile virus infection, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The virus enters the body during a mosquito bite, so the first host cells it meets sit in the skin, then in the nearest lymph node. Two cell types, macrophages and dendritic cells, are key early responders in the defence against this virus.

The team found that spit from Aedes aegypti changes how white blood cells are called in, and how the presenting cells send signals, once infection starts. In short, the bite itself tilts the early fight. Tests of vaccines that skip the spit may miss part of the real story.
plos-pone-0011804:
Juan Rodriguez-Paris and co-authors judged a screening chip for inherited hearing loss, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Testing a child born with hearing loss most often starts with one gene, GJB2. If the cause is not found there, more genes are checked one by one, which is slow and costly, since so many gene faults can play a part.

The team weighed an array that tests close to two hundred known faults at once, for its worth in real clinics. For clinics, the study answers a plain question: should this chip join routine testing or not? A sound panel could cut short the long hunt that deaf children and their families face.
plos-pone-0011904:
Jun Liu and co-authors traced in 2010 the evolution of tetherin, a primate protein that traps newly made viruses at the cell surface. Tetherin blocks HIV-1 particles from being released unless the virus's Vpu protein counters it. Similar host defenders, such as APOBEC3G and TRIM5a, carry signs of long arms races with viruses.

Comparing tetherin across primates shows how its sequence changed under that pressure. Fast change in the parts viruses touch is a signature of repeated attack and defense over millions of years. Reading that history in primates, our close relatives, helps explain why some animal viruses jump to humans more easily than others.
plos-pone-0012004:
Eric Weaver published in 2010 a detailed family tree of the cat AIDS virus across the United States. Feline immunodeficiency virus causes AIDS-like illness in cats and serves as a working model for HIV. Like HIV, it keeps diverging as it spreads, so isolates differ more with time and distance.

A detailed phylogenetic analysis sorts those isolates into their true relationships, showing how the virus entered and diversified within the country. Such trees guide the choice of strains for vaccine and diagnostic work, since a test built on one branch may miss another. They also give veterinarians a map of what is actually circulating in American cats.
plos-pone-0012104:
Daudi Simba, Marian Warsame, Deodatus Kakoko, and colleagues reported a community study from rural Tanzania in PLOS ONE in 2010. Malaria can be cured with modern combination drugs, but only when sick children get them fast. Tanzania had adopted those drugs as standard care, yet cost and supply problems kept them out of reach for many families in the countryside.

The team followed children in the Kilosa area to see who actually got the new treatment quickly, and who did not. Work like this shows the gap between a policy on paper and medicine in a child's hands. It points health programs at the real barriers, such as price, distance, and stock, that decide whether a cure arrives in time.
plos-pone-0012204:
Eleonora Dehlink, Alexandra Baker, Elizabeth Yen, and co-authors measured allergy antibody in children's blood for PLOS ONE in 2010. IgE, the antibody behind immediate allergic reactions, is usually measured free in the blood serum, and high levels flag allergy. But much of the body's IgE sits bound to receptors on cell surfaces, invisible to the standard test, so serum levels may not tell the whole story.

The team measured serum IgE, cell-bound IgE, and the receptors themselves in children, and mapped how the three relate. If bound IgE follows different rules, allergy testing may be missing part of the signal. A fuller picture could refine diagnosis in children whose symptoms and serum tests disagree.
plos-pone-0012304:
Iskandar Abdullaev, Alena Rudkouskaya, and Alexander Mongin tested ion channels in glioma brain tumors, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Gliomas are among the most treatment-resistant cancers, and some evidence blamed two potassium channels, opened by calcium, for helping tumor cells multiply so relentlessly. Other studies disagreed, leaving the channels' guilt in doubt.

The team confirmed both channels do work in human glioma cells, yet blocking them did not govern the cells' proliferation. That negative result saves the field from chasing the wrong lever for growth, while leaving open other roles, such as movement, for the channels. In a cancer this desperate for targets, ruling one out cleanly is real progress.
plos-pone-0012404:
Meredith Shaffer, Yanping Huang, Evann Corbo and colleagues asked whether a plentiful T cell protein is truly needed, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Ezrin links cargo to the cell's inner skeleton and is packed into young thymus cells that mature into T cells. Its abundance suggested a key job in T cell development, but presence alone does not prove need.

Mice lacking ezrin still built T cells normally, the team found. Backup proteins likely cover its absence in this setting. The negative result is valuable: it stops labs from chasing a dead end and redirects attention to the settings, such as cell movement, where ezrin may truly be required.
plos-pone-0012504:
Marika Olcott, Marcella Henkels, Kise Rosen and colleagues fed fruit fly larvae selected strains of a common soil bacterium, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Pseudomonas fluorescens strains live around plant roots and some are sold to protect crops. The fruit fly is a standard stand-in for probing how microbes affect animal bodies, and larvae offer a fast, sensitive test.

Some strains killed larvae or delayed their development, while others were far gentler. Strain-level differences mean a species name alone cannot vouch for safety. The fly assay gives regulators and growers a quick screen before bacterial products are spread widely on food crops.
plos-pone-0012604:
Wilkinson, Solan, Taylor and co-authors asked whether variety within one species matters for an ecosystem. Most biodiversity research counts species, not the genetic variety inside each one. Their 2010 study used fungi, which break down dead matter and release carbon as they grow.

They varied how much genetic diversity the fungi carried and then measured growth and breathing rate. Diversity inside the species changed both, so a single-species view can miss real effects. The lesson reaches beyond fungi, since microbes drive soil and carbon cycles everywhere. Protecting variety within species may matter as much as protecting species counts.
plos-pone-0012704:
Sun, Errami, Long and co-authors measured how alike full-text biomedical papers can be, beyond simple copying checks. Software had been used to find duplicate papers in the MEDLINE index, mostly from titles and summaries. Their 2010 study worked with complete articles, which are now widely available online.

They characterised text similarity across whole papers in a systematic way. Strong overlap can flag plagiarism, honest reuse of methods text, or duplicate publication, and the three need telling apart. Better measures help journals and indexers police the literature without false alarms.
plos-pone-0012804:
Zhao, Ayoub and Hayashi located the silk genes of widow spiders on their chromosomes. Spider dragline silk is famed for being both strong and tough for its weight. It is made of two proteins, MaSp1 and MaSp2, spun into the frame lines of webs and the spider's safety line.

Their 2010 mapping placed the genes for these proteins in the widow spider genome. Gene position helps explain how the pair is switched on together during spinning. The work supports efforts to copy spider silk for medical and engineering uses.  The mapping used labelled DNA probes on spread chromosomes.
pmc-4455604:
Heberle, Meirelles, da Silva, and their team built InteractiVenn in 2015. Comparing sets is a step in a huge number of data workflows, above all in biology. Venn diagrams are the standard display for such comparisons, but existing tools were limited in what they allowed.

InteractiVenn is a web-based tool that lets users work with set diagrams in a flexible way. Users can build diagrams with several sets, edit labels, and pull out the members of any overlap. That interactivity turns a static figure into a working view of the data. It speeds the common task of finding what gene lists or sample groups share.
pmc-4531804:
Emms and Kelly made OrthoFinder in 2015, a tool for work on whole genomes. Genes in two species that came from one gene in a shared past form groups. Labs sort genes into such groups to compare species and trace how gene sets change over time.

The team found a flaw no one had seen in how old tools built these groups. Long genes skewed the groups and made them less true. OrthoFinder fixes that length bias with a new method. Tests showed the groups it builds are far more sound. Clean gene groups are a base step for work on gene birth, loss, and change.
pmc-4595904:
Wick, Schultz, Zobel, and their colleagues built Bandage in 2015 for genome assembly work. When a genome is assembled from scratch, the result is a graph of contigs, or nodes, joined by edges. Users found those connections hard to reach and inspect with existing tools.

Bandage draws assembly graphs in an interactive way, so users can navigate them easily. Seeing the graph helps spot tangles, repeats, and possible errors that tables hide. That visual check can rescue an assembly or explain why it broke at a point. The tool gave genome researchers a practical way to explore the structures their assemblers produce.
pmc-4756104:
Ríos-Covián, Ruas-Madiedo, Margolles, and their co-authors reviewed short chain fatty acids in the gut in 2016. The colon holds a dense population of microbes, the gut microbiota. These microbes break down carbs and proteins that the small intestine leaves behind.

Among their products are short chain fatty acids, which feed colon cells and signal to the immune system. The review links diet to the production of these acids and to human health. What people eat shapes which microbes thrive and what they release. That chain from diet to microbes to body chemistry is now central to nutrition science.
pmc-5576104:
Weiner, Lewis, Stanick, and their team tested new measures in 2017 for implementation research. Such measures track whether efforts to put proven care into practice are working. The measures in use lacked clear concepts, and their quality was largely unknown.

The team built three new measures and tested them for soundness. They cover how staff judge a new practice: whether it is acceptable, a good fit, and feasible to run. Tested tools let teams compare rollout plans on equal terms. Without them, a failed launch could be blamed on the care itself, when the true fault lay in how it was brought in.
pmc-7067204:
