Jasper Chan, Kin-Hang Kok, Zheng Zhu, and coauthors characterized the genome of the new coronavirus in early 2020. A mysterious outbreak of pneumonia appeared in Wuhan in late 2019 and was linked to a seafood market. Within weeks a novel coronavirus was named as the cause.

The team sequenced the virus from a patient with atypical pneumonia and compared it with known coronaviruses. It proved closest to bat coronaviruses and distinct from the earlier SARS virus. Its entry protein suggested strong ability to infect human cells. The analysis helped confirm the outbreak's source family in the pandemic's opening weeks.
pmc-7418704:
Tyler Starr and co-authors measured in 2020 how every possible small change to a key piece of the COVID-19 virus affects its behavior. Their focus was the receptor binding domain, the part of the viral spike that grips the human ACE2 receptor. This piece is also a main target of the antibodies people make against the virus.

Using a method that builds and tests thousands of altered versions at once, they measured how each change affected the protein's folding and its grip on the receptor. The resulting map shows which spots cannot change without breaking the virus, and which can shift freely. Vaccine and drug designers use such maps to anticipate how the virus might evolve to escape treatment.
pmc-7779004:
Damian Szklarczyk and colleagues presented the 2021 edition of the STRING database, a resource for mapping how proteins work together. Life inside a cell depends on a web of partnerships between proteins, which pass signals, build structures, and run chemistry as teams. STRING gathers known and predicted protein associations from many sources into one network that researchers can explore.

The update adds flexible ways to customize the networks and a feature for characterizing sets of genes or measurements that users upload themselves. That lets a researcher move from a raw list of results to a picture of the processes involved. STRING is one of the standard first stops when making sense of gene level data.
plos-pone-0360404:
Xingguang Li and five colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It traces HIV-1 CRF01_AE, one named strain family of the virus that causes AIDS. The authors follow how this strain has spread around the world and how it has changed over time.

Their evidence comes from phylogenetic analysis, which builds family trees from virus gene sequences to show how samples relate. Those trees reveal routes of spread and branching patterns in the strain's history. Public health researchers use such reconstructions to understand epidemics and to keep vaccine and testing work matched to the viruses actually circulating.
plos-pone-0359404:
Zongcheng Hu and Li Shao wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about the Chinese Baroque Historic Area, a district famous for its blend of Chinese and Western building styles. The authors trace how the narratives of place identity have evolved, the stories told about what the district is and means.

Their method follows long-term textual practices, how writing about the area has presented it across many years. Place identity guides tourism, preservation, and residents' pride, and it is built partly through repeated texts. Heritage managers and city marketers are the readers for a history of how one district's story has been written.
plos-pone-0359304: Kuchynka and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on signaling proteins filmed inside living cells. G proteins relay signals from the cell surface inward. The team tracked one form built from G-beta-1 and gamma-2 parts and found its movement differs by subtype. How fast these relays drift can change how long a signal lasts, a detail drug designers care about.
plos-pone-0355104:
Isaac Ogloblin Ramirez and six colleagues reconstruct daily work at an ancient industrial site in Israel, in a 2026 PLOS ONE article. Tel Shiqmona held a vast Iron Age works for purple dye, unmatched in size around the Mediterranean, and the Kingdom of Israel ran it as a state asset. Scholars often picture such workshops as fixed spaces with one job, and the team tested that assumption on the eighth century BCE level.

Using microscope scale soil analysis and chemical spectroscopy, they found the same rooms served different trades at different times of year. Olive pressing fit late autumn, sheltering livestock fit winter, and textile work fit spring, with dye making slotted into the gaps. Ash was spread to freshen floors between seasons. The pattern points to careful, scheduled management of a valuable royal facility.
europmc-pmc7292504: Walker and co-authors published this research paper in 2020 on the impact of COVID-19 and plans for mitigation and suppression in low and middle-income countries. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.

History written as hero-worship, and the longest biography in the language. Not quick reading, but an unforgettable immersion.
the-works-of-samuel-johnson-in-sixteen-v: Volume four of Samuel Johnson's works: essays, criticism, and the great moralist's judgments on literature and life. The Rambler and Idler papers show his mind at its most vigorous. The foundation of English criticism. Johnson's Dictionary alone would immortalize him; these works show the rest.
original-short-stories-volume-04: Guy de Maupassant's short stories, volume four: tales of Paris and the provinces. The master's irony at full strength. Perfect short fiction. Fourth volume: Paris and provinces, irony at full strength, perfect tales, tales of Paris.
the-wandering-jew-volume-04: Eugène Sue’s fourth volume of the Wandering Jew gathers the heirs. The Rennepont family’s fate hangs in the balance. The great melodrama rolls ever onward. Suspense and sensation on every page, Eugène Sue.
memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volume-04: Volume four covers the Empire in its shining years. Victories abroad and splendor at home fill Bourrienne's pages. The secretary notes both the triumphs and the first cracks. A vivid record of Napoleon at his peak.
recollections-of-the-private-life-of-nap: Louis Constant, Napoleon's valet, shares his private memories in volume four. He saw the emperor at table, at work, and at rest. Small details paint a human picture of the great man. An intimate backstage view of history.
essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volume-04: Volume four of the Essays turns to friendship and loss. Montaigne writes of his beloved friend La Boetie with aching tenderness. These are among the most loved pages ever written. Grief made noble by a great mind.
coniston-volume-04: The fourth volume of Churchill's Coniston moves toward its close. Small-town politics reach their decisive hour in New Hampshire. The honest hero faces his greatest trial. A satisfying end to a fine American novel.
the-confessions-of-jean-jacques-rousseau: The fourth volume of the Confessions brings young Rousseau to Paris. The unknown musician meets Diderot and the brilliant philosophes. Ambition and awkwardness mark his difficult early days. A rare genius struggling toward the light.
serge-panine-volume-04: The fourth volume of Serge Panine brings the drama to a head. The heartless villain's elaborate plots unravel toward exposure. Justice and outraged passion collide at last. A rousing close to a very popular novel.
plos-pone-0357004:
Marion C Aichberger and five colleagues ask whether experiencing ethnic discrimination soured people on digital contact tracing, in PLOS ONE in 2026. App based tracing during COVID-19 only works if the public trusts the state behind it. The team surveyed a quota sample of seven hundred German residents in September 2020 and modeled how discrimination experiences flowed through privacy fears, trust, and solidarity into support for the tool.

The models confirmed the worry: discrimination predicted lower support and lower willingness to opt in, carried by privacy concerns and weaker trust in government. Solidarity, the hoped for bridge, did not explain the link. Among non users, fear that the government might turn tracing data against their own ethnic group specifically reduced future willingness. The authors say disease control tools must be designed with minority communities' justified mistrust in view.
plos-pone-0354604:
Wei Gou leads a team of seven reading the full length message molecules of artery cells exposed to cigarette smoke, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Using long read sequencing on human aortic smooth muscle cells, they captured complete RNA transcripts rather than fragments, letting them see edited and spliced variants that short reads miss. A puzzle framed the work: weak smoke extract slightly boosted cell survival in their tests, while stronger doses killed in proportion.

At the mid strength dose they catalogued more than eleven thousand previously unknown transcripts. Activated messages clustered in cell division and in ferroptosis, an iron driven death pathway, while energy production and antioxidant defense messages fell. Hundreds of splicing changes touched cell cycle regulators. The authors argue that smoke's damage is executed through coordinated rewriting of the cell's message library, an isoform level view of how smoking injures blood vessels.
plos-pone-0354304:
Raed M Ennab, writing alone in PLOS ONE in 2026, runs a fair race between four heart disease classifiers on synthetic data. The dataset is a large competition file of six hundred thirty thousand artificial patients, not real ones, built for model comparison. All four algorithms, from logistic regression to three boosted tree systems, faced identical cross validation splits. Preprocessing stayed locked inside each training fold. Traps were set to catch information leaking from the answers.

The race ended nearly in a dead heat. The best tree system edged the field by a hair; logistic regression trailed by only a few thousandths on the headline discrimination score. Calibration was excellent across the board, and the leakage traps came back clean. Ennab's point is the frame itself: synthetic benchmarks can rank algorithms honestly, but their scores say nothing about performance on real clinic patients, a caveat vendors prefer to skip.
plos-pone-0347004:
Edna Judith Márquez leads a team of four uncovering hidden species inside a common Colombian river fish, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The fish, an Astyanax tetra from the Magdalena basin, has long been filed under one uncertain name. The stakes are practical: the Ituango dam now cuts the Cauca River, and conservation cannot protect what taxonomy cannot see. The team characterized seventeen genetic markers and sampled across the river's middle and lower reaches.

Genetics split the fish into two groups, and family tree analyses of two further genes backed the split as distinct lineages. Unexpectedly, one lineage clustered with relatives from the Maracaibo basin, not with its river mates. Body shape analysis agreed that the groups differ. Both carried genetic diversity alongside signs of recent population crashes and inbreeding. A fish treated as one widespread species is at least two, and each half needs its own protection plan.
plos-pone-0357404:
Stephanie Casey and colleagues published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE reporting hard lessons from attempts to clean DDT out of old soil using white-rot fungi. DDT, a banned pesticide, lingers for decades; fungi such as the oyster mushroom can break down similar pollutants in labs. The team tried two realistic approaches: mixing spent mushroom-growing material straight into contaminated soil in pots, and adding fungus-grown substrate to soil at a field site.

Neither approach produced any measurable drop in DDT or its breakdown products. The fungi struggled to survive and spread through real, aged soil, unlike the freshly spiked soils used in many earlier lab successes. Rather than hiding a negative result, the authors map what limited performance: fungal survival, substrate quality, and poor colonization. The account gives future cleanup projects a realistic checklist of what must be fixed before mushroom-based treatment can work outside the lab.
plos-pone-0357904:
Justin Clements and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE measuring PCBs, the banned industrial chemicals that linger for decades, in wildlife across northern New Mexico. Animals were collected opportunistically over fifteen-plus years and grouped by diet: meat eaters, plant eaters, and omnivores. The team compared total contamination, chemical family profiles, and the dioxin-like fraction that drives much of the toxicity.

Carnivores carried the heaviest PCB loads and the highest toxic equivalents, consistent with the chemicals concentrating up the food chain. Mountain lions held more than their main prey, mule deer and elk, a direct demonstration of that magnification. Deer and elk sampled near developed areas were also more contaminated than rural counterparts. Production was banned in the nineteen seventies, so these are legacy pollutants from old equipment and materials still leaking into food webs, with top predators the clearest sentinels.
plos-pone-0354204:
Konstantinos Karagiorgos and co-authors simulate how river flooding breaks a city's road network, hunting for failure patterns that simple damage counts miss. Roads are a city's lifelines, and floods cut them in tangled ways. Their method blends classic network measures of how connected and central streets are. It adds community detection. Then it floods the network twice: under a rare flood, and under an extreme near-worst-case flood drawn from Swedish planning practice.

Damage grew in jumps, not smoothly. The network split into a few large islands plus hundreds of small cut-off fragments. Average travel burden more than doubled under the larger flood. The analysis also named isolated high-risk nodes and streets that could serve as evacuation corridors. Karagiorgos and colleagues offer the framework to any flood-prone city.
plos-pone-0357104:
Nataly Rodríguez-Lugo and colleagues catalog the bacteria and fungi living inside the roots of an endangered bromeliad in Colombia's high páramo, a cold tropical ecosystem under climate pressure. Root microbes can make or break a rare plant's survival, and this species' partners were unknown. Using long-read gene sequencing on root tissue and surrounding soil, the team compared who lives where and what jobs they likely do.

Root communities were less diverse than soil but more tightly interwoven, rich in acid-loving and nitrogen-fixing partners, while soils carried the region's usual microbes and more nutrient cycling roles. Both held fungi that feed on dead matter plus some known plant pathogens. Rodríguez-Lugo and colleagues say conservation for this bromeliad should plan around its root partners, not just the plant.
plos-pone-0356904:
Delia Akosua Bandoh and a Ghanaian team test stool from toddlers with diarrhea in a coastal district where rotavirus vaccine coverage is high, asking what germs fill the gap the vaccine left. Diarrhea still burdens young children, and its causes are shifting. A few dozen children under five at a district facility gave samples checked by rapid tests and a broad gene panel, with illness severity scored on a standard scale.

Rotavirus itself appeared in only a single case. Two bacterial types dominated instead, one in about half the children and a combined shigella-type signal in about three quarters, with norovirus the leading virus. Nearly every child carried more than one germ, and mixed bacterial-viral infections leaned more severe. Bandoh and colleagues urge routine pathogen surveillance to keep guiding treatment.
plos-pone-0355204:
Susana Carvalho and a large team recorded bearded capuchin monkeys in northeastern Brazil hunting and eating small vertebrates across forty-five months, the most extensive record of its kind for these monkeys. Their 2026 study of two neighboring groups weighed how provisioning by humans, sex, age, fruit and insect supplies, and weather shaped how often the monkeys caught mammals and lizards.

Vertebrate eating proved habitual, not desperate. Males and adults hunted most, brains and organs were eaten first, and predation rose when fruit ran short while dropping when humans provisioned the monkeys. The authors argue such small-prey habits may have been the stepping stone that led early human ancestors toward larger game, and suggest re-examining fossil bone collections for overlooked small prey.
plos-pone-0356604:
Janny Mathieu and colleagues ran a randomized trial on a simple question. Does telling a spine surgeon what an expert triage clinician found change anything for back pain patients? Their 2026 study enrolled 101 adults referred for a surgical consultation. Everyone received a standardized assessment from a chiropractor. But for half the patients, the findings were shared with the surgeon beforehand.

Patients reported pain, disability, quality of life, and care paths over twelve months. The authors expected equal pain outcomes with smoother journeys through care. But proof of equivalence on the main pain measure was not established at the three-month check. The trial tests a practical reshaping of spine care. It uses spine experts as informed gatekeepers to scarce surgical time.
plos-pone-0356004: Carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas and Enterobacterales are nightmare bacteria — but new drug combinations offer hope. This reference-laboratory study examined carbapenem resistance alongside susceptibility to ceftazidime/avibactam and ceftolozane/tazobactam. The susceptibility data guide last-resort antibiotic choices.
plos-pone-0355604:
Le Huu Binh, Thuy-Van Duong, and Duc Huy Le present a learning-based method for organizing wireless sensor networks in this 2026 paper. In software-defined sensor networks for the Internet of Things, each node's radio range shapes the whole network's energy use and reliability. The goal is for every node to end up with a sensible number of neighbors. Their algorithm lets each node adjust its own range using reinforcement learning. A second learning model at the central controller picks which node learns next. The nodes share lessons without sharing raw data.

In simulations, the federated approach hit the target neighbor counts more accurately than well-known topology control algorithms, while also using less energy and delivering better transmission quality. The authors argue that splitting learning between nodes and controller suits networks too large and too privacy-sensitive for purely central control.
plos-pone-0355504:
Tianle Duan and co-authors linked the density of physical establishments in American counties with rates of hearing difficulty. Hearing research usually stops at body and income factors. Their 2026 study mapped shops, services, and similar establishments against hearing data across counties and over time.

Raw comparisons suggested denser counties hear better. Those counties also had denser roads, higher status, younger residents, and better schooling and insurance. Once road density and social factors were held constant, the link flipped: denser establishments then came with more hearing difficulty. The authors credit road networks, as a proxy for access and connectivity, with driving the reversal. They also flag specific establishment types as hearing-health risks.
plos-pone-0354804:
Yan Mou, Zhaolong Gao, and Jinjiang Li present in 2026 a vision system for picking out the main object in underwater scenes. The task supports tracking, editing, and recognition, but water muddies colour and depth readings. Their network fuses colour and depth data through attention steps that inject and embed features across both channel and space views.

By modelling how the two data types complete each other at wide and narrow scales, the system sharpens standout regions and quiets background noise. Layered fusion also lessens depth errors. Tests on several underwater sets beat leading methods, the authors report, showing the value of careful fusion.
plos-pone-0355304:
Tianfu Huang builds in 2026 a learning system to forecast when smart meter sensors on a Chinese island will drift out of accuracy. Salt fog, damp air, and heating and cooling cycles corrode the parts that measure power. Six years of field records from hundreds of sensors trained a combined model that joins several network types with a swarm based weighting step.

The combined forecaster beat its best single part and explained most of the variation in drift. Two new indices captured salt build up and corrosion drive, and the clash of load current with temperature emerged as the top drift cause. In field use the system warned days ahead.
plos-pone-0353704:
Manish Barik and co-authors track chewing tobacco trends in 2026. They used three national family health surveys from India. The surveys span about fifteen years. All women were aged fifteen to forty nine. Such products raise oral cancer risk and harm health in other ways, and India holds most of the world's users. Each survey round was analysed apart, with layered models searching for who uses these products.

Use fell steadily across the rounds, from a high single digit share to a lower one. A flavoured chew mix stayed the most common form, and one northeastern state kept by far the highest rate. Low schooling, older age, caste, region, and smoking inside the home all linked to use.
plos-pone-0354904:
Jaime Banks, Jonathan Stromer-Galley, Samiksha Singh, and Collin Capano published this 2026 paper introducing DiSCoKit, free open-source software for survey research with live chatbots. Studies of how people interact with large language models need participants to chat with a real model inside a survey, which survey platforms make awkward.

DiSCoKit plugs live model sessions into tools like Qualtrics, logs the conversations, and lets researchers steer the model's behavior for experiments. Banks and colleagues walk through the design, a sample deployment, and the toolkit's limits. Their goal is to give social scientists a safer, roomier way to study human and AI interaction.
plos-pone-0354704:
Noura Alsufyani, Sawsan Alowa, Hend Alrasheed, and Sakher Alqahtani published this 2026 forensic study of estimating legal age from dental X-rays. Whether someone is under or over eighteen matters in court, and wisdom teeth are still developing at that age. Using nearly six hundred panoramic images of teenagers and young adults, they trained machine learning to segment the tooth and classify age.

Their best model judged the age line with high accuracy, edging past manual expert scoring on several measures. Alsufyani suggests pixel-level analysis catches subtle cues that human readers miss.
plos-pone-0353504:
Soltanabadi and colleagues, in a 2026 review, ask how far neck movement relates to pain and disability in people with neck pain. Clinicians often measure how far a patient can turn or tilt the neck, assuming tighter movement means worse symptoms. The team gathered every study that linked that movement measure to patient-reported pain or disability.

Forty-five studies, with about three and a half thousand patients in total, were combined in statistical summaries. Movement in every direction showed a modest link with symptoms: less movement went with somewhat more pain and disability. The link was stronger for fresh injuries and for whiplash from crashes than for long-lasting or non-injury pain. Study quality varied a lot, and the authors rate the overall certainty as very low. They call for standard ways to measure neck movement and stronger studies before clinics lean too hard on this measure.
plos-pone-0352204:
Adams and colleagues, in a 2026 study, turn North Carolina residents into partners in tick research. Tick-borne disease is rising in the state, yet local data are thin. Working with twenty-two county health agencies, the team handed out kits so people could send in ticks they found, along with notes on where and what they were doing.

Over two years, more than four hundred ticks arrived. Testing checked them for several bacterial germs, including the one that causes Lyme disease. Species matched earlier records, with one surprise: a lone star tick turned up in the cool mountains, the first published record there, hinting at a push into higher ground. Recreation, such as hiking and yard leisure, was the activity most tied to encounters. How counties advertised the program affected returns, though numbers were small. The authors offer the project as a model for cheap disease tracking.
plos-pone-0353204:
Cai compared artery-clearing treatment for two kinds of severe stroke in a 2026 study. One kind blocks an artery at the back of the brain and often causes deep disability or death. Both groups had scans that map blood flow to guide treatment, drawn from a shared international registry.

Patients with the back-brain blockage arrived with worse symptoms than the comparison group. After careful matching of similar patients, recovery and death rates at three months looked much the same in both groups. The back-brain group even had faster reopening and fewer bleeding problems. Scan-guided selection may help these patients gain the same benefit as others.
plos-pone-0352804:
Reza Sharifi and four colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One analysis of cleft lip and palate in Iran, drawn from the Global Burden of Disease study. These birth conditions affect feeding, speech, and appearance across a lifetime, and Iran lacked an up-to-date national picture. The authors estimated new cases, existing cases, deaths, and years of healthy life lost for the whole country and all thirty-one provinces between 1990 and 2023.

Deaths and disability from clefts fell dramatically over those three decades, dropping by roughly nine-tenths, while the share of people living with the condition stayed broadly steady. Tehran showed the highest prevalence and Isfahan the lowest, and children under five carried the greatest burden. Provinces with stronger social development generally had lower disability rates, and the authors call for sustained early detection and specialist care.
plos-pone-0352504:
Cherry Kim and seven colleagues evaluate this 2026 PLOS One imaging study on spotting anemia from CT scans that patients are already having for other reasons. A dual-energy CT technique can estimate the electron density of blood, which should fall as red cell mass drops. The team analyzed more than twenty-five hundred scans, with and without contrast dye, comparing blood-pool measurements against laboratory blood counts.

Electron density fell steadily as anemia worsened and correlated strongly with hemoglobin on scans without contrast, where it detected anemia accurately. On contrast scans the link survived while the ordinary brightness measure used by radiologists showed none. The authors frame contrast-scan detection as opportunistic, useful mainly for catching severe anemia incidentally, and say the approach needs testing on other scanner brands.
plos-pone-0352604:
Hong Yang and seven co-authors present a 2026 mouse study of pachymic acid, a compound from a medicinal fungus. They test its effects on body clocks disturbed by obesity. A high-fat diet upsets daily rhythms as well as weight and blood sugar. The compound had never been tested for rhythm effects.

Mice given the compound gained less weight, handled glucose and fats better, and recovered steadier daily patterns of melatonin and body temperature. Gene activity in the liver also fell back into a normal daily cycle. The team traces the benefit to a fat-signalling pathway in the liver. It involves a receptor called S1PR4. That pathway could become a target for treating rhythm problems linked with obesity.
plos-pone-0352904:
Tigist Alemu and four colleagues analyse maternal deaths in an Ethiopian intensive care unit. Their 2026 study covers a tertiary hospital in the country's south. It follows three hundred seventy-eight obstetric patients admitted to intensive care over ten years. The question is not only how many mothers died, but how fast, and what predicted it.

One hundred twenty-six of the women died. More than seven in ten deaths came within the first five days. Half of all deaths had occurred by roughly the third day. Living in a rural area raised the risk. So did shock, multi-organ failure, and needing a breathing machine. Impaired consciousness was the strongest warning sign of all. The message is stark: survival is decided in the first days, so rural referral speed and early resuscitation matter most.
plos-pone-0351704:
Making heart muscle cells from stem cells in the lab is slow and the cells stay immature. Agatha Ribeiro Kalthof and colleagues found that switching off a gene called IRX3 speeds the process, in this 2026 PLOS One study using human induced stem cells.

Cells lacking the gene turned into heart cells in greater numbers and switched on mature heart genes more strongly. Their electrical behavior improved, energy factories spread more evenly, and the striped muscle fibers organized better. Early in the process, partner genes that drive heart development rose, and young heart cells multiplied faster. The finding may help labs grow better heart tissue for disease models and repair research.
plos-pone-0351504:
How people bond in close relationships shapes who they feel they are, and Cui Lyu and colleagues mapped those links in six hundred twenty-four Chinese college students. Their 2026 PLOS One study drew the connections as a network rather than simple pairs, and compared men's and women's maps.

Identity questions clustered tightly together. A feeling that time and selfhood are coming apart formed the main bridge between attachment and identity, followed by a scattered sense of self. Anxious attachment was the strongest single bridge on the relationship side. Overall network structure did not differ by gender, though women's connections ran slightly stronger in total.
plos-pone-0351404:
Zebrafish larvae are favorite stand-ins for studying the human heart, but labs measure them at different ages and conditions. Patricia Fiorino and colleagues charted how the larval heart changes hour by hour, in this 2026 PLOS One study, and tested how temperature and water acidity sway the readings.

Heart rate, output, and the fraction of blood pumped were measured at eight ages from one to just over three days after fertilization. Heart rate climbed until about three days, then leveled. Output rose in two bursts, while the pumped fraction mostly held steady with one brief dip. Small temperature and acidity shifts moved the numbers, so the authors urge standard settings.
plos-pone-0351304:
Quick HIV viral load testing near the clinic, rather than at a distant central lab, returns results faster for children and young people. Perry Msoka and colleagues watched clinics and interviewed health workers in Tanzania to find where the near-site system jams, in this 2026 PLOS One qualitative study.

The work formed part of a four-country East African trial testing young people at three points across a year. Observations from 2023 into 2024 captured daily friction: machine downtime, supply gaps, staffing, and result hand-offs among the suspects. Naming the bottlenecks matters because the technology's speed only helps if samples, staff, and results actually flow, the authors argue.
plos-pone-0348504:
Haruka Nagaya and colleagues linked blood vitamin C levels with brain scans in just over two thousand older adults. Vitamin C in food has been tied to lower risk of thinking decline, yet direct links to brain structure were unclear. Scans measured grey and white matter volumes and the strength of a key resting brain network, with many health and habit factors counted.

Low vitamin C in blood went with a lower share of grey matter and weaker network links, even after age, schooling, illness, smoking, drinking, and activity were taken into account. A snapshot cannot prove that vitamin C protects the brain. Still, the tight link in a large group makes diet and brain ageing worth closer, longer study.
plos-pone-0349804:
Eric M Mortensen, Nkiruka Atuegwu, and Shane J Sacco tested whether fancy learning models beat plain regression at predicting return to hospital within thirty days after pneumonia. Records covered just over twenty seven hundred adults at one academic centre from 2018 to 2024, with full vital sign values kept as continuous inputs rather than cut into bands.

About ten percent returned within thirty days. Gradient boosting and neural nets scored about the same as plain regression on both accuracy scales. Drug abuse history and a kidney lab value emerged as underused predictors. Extra model complexity bought nothing here; better data and follow up design may matter more than smarter maths.
plos-pone-0350004:
Alexandra Gaal Kovalcikova and colleagues tested whether white cell nets drive kidney damage in a mouse model of chronic kidney disease. Nets are webs of DNA that immune cells cast out, suspected of harming tissue. Mice lacking the enzyme that enables net making were compared with normal mice, both dosed with a kidney harming chemical for two weeks.

Chemical dosing shrank body weight and worsened kidney markers sharply in normal mice. Knockout mice fared no better, and even showed an earlier rise in one kidney marker. Immune cells were clearly activated, yet net making itself did not drive damage in this model. Kidney researchers should look elsewhere for this models main harm path.
plos-pone-0350804:
Yongping Yu and fellow researchers in China tackled a practical fire safety problem in 2026: which factors matter most when a building catches fire. Many things can start or spread a blaze, and naming the few that drive the rest helps prevention work.

The team turned past fire cases into a network, where each factor was a node and links showed factors that appeared together. Their new method weighed a node's place in the core, its reach, and how hard it would be to replace. That ranking points safety teams toward the controls likely to cut risk most, rather than spreading effort thinly over every possible cause.
plos-pone-0350204:
Allison K White, Md Saydur Rahman, and Richard J Kline measured fish at a human-made reef off the Texas coast in 2026. The reef, built from recycled and shaped materials, covers a large area and draws fish, but its value needed numbers.

Using a sonar that splits its beam to size echoes, the team estimated fish weight at sites of different heights and worked out how much carbon those fish hold. Fish were far more plentiful than over bare sandy bottom. Counts like these help judge whether built reefs truly support fisheries, and whether the fish they hold store a meaningful share of carbon.
plos-pone-0349504:
Qianqian Sun and colleagues checked a World Health Organization rehabilitation scoring set on more than a thousand Chinese cancer patients in 2026. No full scale existed for judging how such patients function during rehabilitation, so a trusted measure had to be proven locally.

Trained staff scored patients, and a smaller group was scored again for consistency checks. Scores held together well, matched other trusted measures of mood, daily living, and general condition, and separated patients sensibly. Factor checks supported the scale's structure. A validated common yardstick lets rehabilitation teams across China compare progress and plan care on shared terms.
plos-pone-0341704:
Michael Jones, Richard Dawson, and Jon Mills offer a new way to build fake populations in 2026. Such populations stand in for real people in models of transport, health, and disasters. Real survey microdata is scarce and locked away for privacy. Their method needs none of it.

A large language model invents one household at a time. After each step, the fake population is checked against published totals. Gaps guide the next prompts, so the result drifts toward the targets. No retraining is needed. Tested in many countries, the method matched basic totals closely. It could open population modelling to teams with no access to census files.
plos-pone-0335304:
Kumlachew Geta and co-authors measured how often patients at an Ethiopian referral hospital needed a second abdominal operation after gut surgery, and what raised the odds. Reopening the abdomen carries real risks of harm and death, and it strains hospital budgets and staff. Their 2026 review examined more than twelve hundred patient charts from gastrointestinal procedures performed over two years.

One in ten patients underwent the second operation, a rate above several earlier reports. Prior abdominal surgery stood out as by far the strongest predictor, followed by finding starved, dying bowel during the first operation and needing circulation-supporting drugs during surgery. The authors say flagging these high-risk patients early could focus monitoring and resources where repeat surgery is most likely.
plos-pone-0346704:
Erika Z Chung, Belinda Curpen, and co-authors asked whether ultrasound measurements taken during the first weeks of chemotherapy can forecast how a breast tumor will finally respond. Chemotherapy before surgery is standard for several breast cancer types, but success is only confirmed afterward, too late to spare non-responders needless toxicity. Their 2026 study followed one hundred six patients with ultrasound at six points across treatment.

Patients whose tumors vanished completely showed steep shrinkage in width, area, and volume within the early weeks. Partial responders shrank steadily but less, weak responders barely moved, and non-responders stayed flat throughout. Statistical tests confirmed the early gap between complete responders and the rest. The authors conclude early size change carries real, if imperfect, predictive value for final response.
plos-pone-0349604:
Maura De Coster, Lisette M Kootker, and co-authors read diet history from cremated bones at Nijmegen in the Netherlands, a Roman frontier town where local Batavian life met imperial supply networks. Strontium in bone reflects the geology behind a person's food, and its concentration can hint at salt-rich diets. Their 2026 study compared rural, urban, and military burials from before and during Roman rule.

Urban and military remains carried higher strontium concentrations, consistent with heavier use of salt-preserved foods from Roman provisioning. Northern rural contexts instead showed steady concentrations and narrowing isotope ranges, suggesting local food traditions, possibly including earlier salt habits, persisted. The authors argue dietary change under Rome was patchy and negotiated, not a simple swap of local for imperial food.
plos-pone-0349204:
Cathy Yang and colleagues tested an unusual nerve repair in rats: gluing severed nerve fibers back together with a plastic-like compound called PEG. When a chunk of the sciatic nerve is lost, standard graft repairs regrow slowly and recovery is usually poor. Using grafts from genetically identical rats, the team compared the fusion treatment with ordinary grafting on gaps of two sizes.

The compound seals the cut membranes of nerve fibers almost instantly, which in principle preserves the fibers instead of letting them die back and regrow at a millimeter or two per day. Structure and walking behavior were then tracked to judge recovery. If fusion works reliably, it could change how surgeons treat the worst peripheral nerve injuries.
plos-pone-0349304:
Charlotte Jane Whiffin and a large team explored whether storytelling, guided by an approach called Life Threads, can help families after a relative suffers a traumatic brain injury. Such injuries change family life deeply, yet relatives get little support for their own grief and shock. Twenty family members joined group sessions, used threads and objects to lay out their stories over four weeks, and then spoke at length about the experience.

Most participants said the method let them tell their story in ways ordinary conversation had not, and many reported real benefits, from making sense of events to feeling heard. Success depended on a safe, well-held setting. The authors see promise in the approach and frame this early study as groundwork for larger trials.
plos-pone-0348804:
Peter Persoon asks a quiet question with big consequences: does progress speed up when existing knowledge gets re-sorted into new categories? Ideas are not only created, he notes, but also reinterpreted, and patent offices record that reinterpretation whenever they move a patent into a different class. Using patent records as a stand-in for technical knowledge, he documents two patterns and builds an exact maths model around them.

Newer patents are reclassified more often, and bigger classes absorb a larger share of reclassified patents. The model's further predictions held across all major technology areas, pointing to a strong link between re-sorting and the pace of change. Persoon argues that the shape of technical growth can be explained from inside the knowledge system itself, not only by outside economic forces.
plos-pone-0349404:
Ihssan S Masad and colleagues tested a jelly-like radiation detector designed to check that cancer radiotherapy delivers dose exactly where the plan says. Their hydrogel changes its magnetic properties where radiation lands, so an MRI scan can read the delivered dose in three dimensions. Gels were scanned, irradiated by a robotic radiotherapy system, then scanned again and compared against the treatment computer's calculations.

The gel's dose maps matched the plan closely, especially in the high-dose zone that matters most. A standard agreement test passed more than nine in ten points at every dose level and viewing plane checked. The authors conclude the new gel is a reliable tool for verifying complex treatments before or alongside patient care. A small targeting error there can mean a missed tumour or a burned organ.
plos-pone-0349104:
Hagos T. Atalay, Victoria J. Kain, and Amanda G. Carter gauge how ready health workers in northern Ethiopia feel to support kangaroo care at home. Kangaroo care keeps small babies warm against a parent's chest and saves lives where incubators are scarce. Their 2026 study surveys close to six hundred professionals and also builds a questionnaire to measure readiness itself.

The new questionnaire held together well in testing. Readiness itself was shaky: few workers had read the national guideline, and most had never been trained in the method. More than half said their workplaces lacked support for it. Workers with past hands-on experience felt more positive. Training and backing, the authors argue, must come before home programs can spread.
plos-pone-0342004:
Mohammed Hlayel and co-workers build a fast bridge between factory controllers and their cloud-based digital twins. A digital twin mirrors a real machine so engineers can test changes safely, but the link must answer within a strict timing standard. Their 2026 study connects a common brand of factory controller to cloud software through a live two-way web channel.

The bridge answered in well under the standard's limit on average. It beat three rival connection methods by wide margins on round-trip time. It also held its speed with many users at once in simulated loads. Factories moving toward more human-centered, resilient production could use such links to watch and steer machines from afar.
plos-pone-0344604:
Waqar Rauf Butt and co-workers turn an ordinary smartphone into a pothole measuring tool. Councils struggle to survey road damage because pro gear is costly and manual checks are slow. Their 2026 study pairs phone photos with the depth sensor built into newer phones, guided by a deep learning pipeline that outlines each pothole and refines its depth.

Training used twenty-five thousand photo and depth pairs gathered under mixed road and light conditions. The system beat existing methods on both depth accuracy and outline quality. Cleaner edges after extra processing helped too. A phone in a vehicle could feed cities a live damage map, letting repair crews start with the deepest, riskiest holes.
plos-pone-0348604:
Subeen Kim and co-workers look for frailty risk factors among older Koreans, separately for women and men. Frailty, a state of weakness that invites falls and illness, grows common with age. Their 2026 study draws on six years of national health survey data covering more than six thousand five hundred adults aged sixty-five and over, scored by a standard frailty checklist.

About one in five women was frail, against roughly one in nine men. Smoking and even sharing morning meals with family linked with higher frailty in women, a pattern the authors flag for care. For men, higher income and eating more were protective. Many chronic diseases and poor self-rated health raised risk in both sexes. Prevention, they argue, should be shaped by gender.
plos-pone-0341404:
Anne Schlutt and co-workers build a kinder way to give lab mice repeated injections and blood draws. Handling stress burdens mice and can distort research, and tail handling frightens them most. Their 2026 study designs a short medical training course plus a small tunnel that holds the mouse gently during procedures, tested in a liver cancer model needing many weeks of injections.

Trained mice approached handlers sooner within a few sessions, and the change lasted the whole experiment. Tunnel-treated mice stayed more active after injections and bounced back to normal behavior faster than firmly held ones. Body temperature tracked room conditions more than training. Gentler routines promise better welfare and cleaner data for long studies.
plos-pone-0348404:
Akihiro Ito and co-workers check whether a planned trial comparing two oxygen levels during lung rehabilitation for chronic lung disease can actually be run. Extra oxygen during exercise training should help breathless patients train harder, but the better dose is unknown. Their 2026 pilot runs six patients through both programs in random order, blinded, using a high-flow nose tube.

The walk test could not anchor a sample size for the main trial. One program improved symptom scores more, while the stronger oxygen program built more muscle. Effect sizes now let the team size a full trial around symptom and muscle outcomes. Pilot work like this prevents a large, expensive trial from being built on the wrong yardstick.
plos-pone-0340004:
Eihab Fathelrahman and his team ran a mock bird flu strike on the UAE. They fed facts from forty-six bird farms into a spread model tuned for the land. Then they played four paths. One had no steps at all. The rest used moves curbs, mass shots, or culls of sick farms.

Culls closed the mock strike in sixteen days. That was the shortest run and the least harm of all paths. No steps let it run for twenty-six days. Move curbs oddly stretched it most, to thirty-two days. The team says the dry run lets chiefs weigh cost and gain while calm holds.
plos-pone-0348204:
Waleed Kattan maps where Saudi Arabia's dentists actually work in this 2026 PLOS ONE health policy analysis, using the health ministry's 2023 yearbook across twenty health regions. He compares public against private practice and Saudi against foreign dentists, asking whether the spread matches the goals of the country's Vision 2030 reforms.

The workforce grew to nearly eight dentists per ten thousand people, yet the map is lopsided: small regions such as Al-Bahah are dentist-rich while crowded Makkah has barely half that density. Private practice employs about seventy percent of dentists and clusters in cities, showing the deepest regional inequality. The analysis gives planners hard numbers for steering dentists toward underserved regions.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Angola appears again in Resolution 1404, adopted unanimously on 18 April 2002. Two weeks earlier, the government and UNITA had signed a ceasefire. The war seemed finally over. Still, sanctions on the former rebels remained in force. A monitoring team was tracking how those measures worked.

The Council extended the team's mandate by six months, to 19 October 2002. Four experts would staff it. Within thirty days they owed a detailed plan for their work. Money, diamonds, and arms linked to UNITA topped the list. Periodic reports were required, with a further full report due by 15 October 2002.

The Marshall Islands, a Pacific nation of low atolls, spent decades under United States administration. It moved to self-government under a compact with Washington. Full UN membership was the next step. Resolution 704, adopted without a vote on 9 August 1991, examined its application.

The Council recommended that the General Assembly admit the Republic of the Marshall Islands. Some summaries pair this text with Micronesia's admission. In fact, the text covers the Marshall Islands alone. The Assembly admitted it that September. Membership mattered for a country of scattered islands. The Marshalls gained a platform for issues like nuclear testing's legacy and rising seas.

Guatemala rushed a complaint to the Council in June 1954. Its government said foreign-backed forces were invading the country. The elected president, Jacobo Árbenz, faced a revolt armed and encouraged from abroad. Resolution 104 was adopted unanimously on 20 June 1954, after urgent debate.

The text is brief but pointed. It calls for the immediate end of any action likely to cause bloodshed. It also asks every UN member to give no help to such action. The words were aimed at halting outside support for the invasion. Events moved faster than diplomacy. Árbenz fell within days, starting decades of turmoil in Guatemala.

Senegal accused Portuguese troops of crossing its border in 1965. Portugal still ruled neighboring Guinea-Bissau as a colony. Its forces were fighting independence guerrillas there. Raids and pursuits spilled into Senegalese villages. Resolution 204 was adopted unanimously on 19 May 1965, after both countries argued their cases.

The Council deeply deplored any incursions into Senegal. It repeated its 1963 warning on the same problem. Portugal was asked yet again to stop violating Senegal's sovereignty. The Secretary-General had to follow events and report. The text shows decolonization's wars straining borders across West Africa. Portugal's colonial wars lasted until its own revolution in 1974.

Seven Gulf sheikhdoms joined together as Britain withdrew in 1971. Their new federation, the United Arab Emirates, was proclaimed on 2 December. An application for UN membership followed immediately. Resolution 304 was adopted unanimously on 8 December 1971. The Council needed less than a week to respond.

Members recommended the Emirates' admission to the General Assembly. The Assembly seated the federation the next day. Few new states arrived with such wealth waiting underground. Oil income soon made the Emirates a major donor and investor. The one-line resolution captures the federation's first act of foreign policy: claiming a lawful seat among nations before its first month was out.

A mysterious attack on Benin's capital brings Resolution 404, adopted by consensus on 8 February 1977. Benin had written to the Council about events at Cotonou on 16 January, when an armed group had struck the city and then escaped. Its representative addressed the Council, and the text recalls every member's duty to respect the territory and independence of others.

The Council affirmed that Benin's territorial integrity and political independence must be respected. It decided to send a special mission of three of its own members to Benin to investigate what happened on 16 January, with a report due by the end of February. The Secretary-General was asked to supply whatever help the mission needed.

Lebanon's peacekeepers are kept in place by Resolution 2004, adopted on 30 August 2011 at Beirut's request. The mandate of UNIFIL, the UN Interim Force in Lebanon, was due to run out. The year had brought grave violations of Resolution 1701. They included terrorist attacks on UNIFIL patrols in May and July 2011. Marking of the Blue Line between Israel and Lebanon was still incomplete.

The Council extends UNIFIL's mandate until 31 August 2012 without amendment. It condemns the attacks on peacekeepers in the strongest terms and demands Lebanon finish its investigation and bring the perpetrators to justice. It orders a strategic review of UNIFIL before year's end to make sure the mission is configured for its tasks. It presses the parties to respect the Blue Line, stop all hostilities, and move toward a permanent ceasefire. Israel is again urged to withdraw from northern Ghajar without further delay.

The Al-Qaida and Taliban sanctions regime gets a fairness overhaul in Resolution 1904, adopted on 17 December 2009. Legal challenges to listings had grown, the Council was mid-way through reviewing every name on the Consolidated List, and Al-Qaida kidnappings for ransom were rising.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council continues the asset freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo against listed individuals and entities, confirming the freeze covers ransoms and internet hosting that supports them. Its central reform creates an Office of the Ombudsperson for eighteen months: an independent figure who receives delisting requests from listed people and entities, replacing the Focal Point for this list. Listings must carry public narrative summaries of reasons, states must notify listed persons promptly, and the review of all Consolidated List names must finish by 30 June 2010. The Monitoring Team is extended for eighteen months, with the measures reviewed within eighteen months.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 2504 (XXIV), adopted on 19 November 1969, closed the United Nations chapter on West New Guinea, also called West Irian. In 1962 the Assembly had noted the agreement between Indonesia and the Netherlands on the territory. It had backed the Secretary-General's role under it. A temporary United Nations authority had since run its handover.

The text takes note of the Secretary-General's report on the act of free choice held under the agreement. It thanks him and his staff for finishing their tasks. It also welcomes aid for the territory's growth. It notes Dutch help given with Indonesia, much of it through the Asian Development Bank and United Nations bodies.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Security Council resolution 1104, adopted on 8 April 1997, is a routine step in staffing the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia. The Council had decided to consider the names put forward for judges of the Tribunal, received by the Secretary-General by 13 March 1997. It forwards the list of nominees to the General Assembly, as article 13 of the Tribunal's Statute requires. The Assembly can then elect the judges from it.

Fighting in the Congolese city of Kisangani drives this text of 16 June 2000. Ugandan and Rwandan troops had clashed there again on 5 June, in the middle of Congo's wider war. Reports that Congo's natural wealth was being taken illegally also worried the Council.

The Council said it was outraged by the fighting and by both countries' failure to keep their promises to stop and pull back. It stood behind the Lusaka Ceasefire Agreement and pressed every party to honour it. It also backed the expert panel studying how Congo's resources were being looted, a trade the Council linked to the war dragging on.

A prosecutor is named for the Yugoslavia war crimes court on 4 September 2003. A week before, the Council had split the once-shared prosecutor post in two and set up its own post for the Rwanda court. Acting on the Secretary-General's choice, it named Carla Del Ponte to the Yugoslavia post, to start on 15 September 2003, for a four-year term.

Cyprus's peacekeeping force, UNFICYP, is extended on 15 June 2005 for a further period ending 15 December 2005. A review of the operation had just been completed. The island stayed stable and the Green Line calm, with fewer incidents between the sides, and the Committee on Missing Persons had resumed its work in August 2004.

The mandate is renewed, and the Turkish Cypriot side and Turkish forces are again called on to restore the military position at Strovilia to what it had been before July 2000. Both parties are again called on to treat the missing persons question with urgency and seriousness as a humanitarian matter, and a report on the mission's work is requested.

Timor-Leste gets a new, expanded United Nations mission on 25 August 2006, after the crisis of that year. Violence and political breakdown had displaced large numbers of people, and many weapons remained unaccounted for. A new government had been formed, but the security and humanitarian situation stayed fragile.

The United Nations Integrated Mission in Timor-Leste, UNMIT, is created for an initial six months. It would include up to 1,608 police personnel and a small initial group of 34 military liaison and staff officers, alongside a large civilian team. Its work centres on supporting the government, restoring public security through policing, and helping prepare for the 2007 elections. International security forces already in the country would work alongside it.
un-sc-res-204:
Senegal accused Portuguese troops of crossing its border in 1965. On 19 May 1965 the Security Council heard both governments. It deeply deplored any incursions into Senegalese territory. The Council restated its 1963 resolution on the same quarrel. Portugal ruled neighboring Guinea-Bissau at the time. Armed struggle for that colony's freedom was already under way.

Portugal had to take all effective steps to stop the violations. Senegal's sovereignty and borders had to be respected. The Secretary-General was told to follow events. The vote was unanimous. The text is one of several in which the Council pressed a colonial power over raids linked to liberation wars.
un-sc-res-404:
An armed raid on Benin's capital brought a Security Council mission on 8 February 1977. Benin's chargé d'affaires had written to the Council on 26 January. The attack had hit Cotonou on 16 January 1977, when foreign fighters landed and struck targets in the city before escaping. Benin's permanent representative addressed the Council on the events.

The Council affirmed that Benin's territorial integrity and political independence had to be respected. It decided to send a special mission of three of its members to Benin. The mission would investigate the events of 16 January at Cotonou and report by the end of February 1977. Its members would be named after talks between the Council's president and its members. The Secretary-General was asked to give the mission the help it needed. The Council stayed seized of the question while the inquiry ran.
un-sc-res-2004:
The Security Council turned to Lebanon in Resolution 2004, adopted on 30 August 2011. Lebanon had asked for the peacekeeping force, UNIFIL, to stay one more year unchanged. Grave clashes had broken the calm in May and August 2011. Bomb attacks in May and July had struck the peacekeepers themselves.

The text extends UNIFIL's mandate until 31 August 2012. It condemns the attacks on peacekeepers in the strongest terms. All sides must honor the halt to fighting and respect the Blue Line in full. Israel should pull its army out of northern Ghajar without more delay. A careful review of the force, to fit it best to its tasks, is due before the year ends.
un-sc-res-1904:
Al-Qaida and Taliban sanctions are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1904, adopted on 17 December 2009. Ten years had passed since the first sanctions text. Courts and listed people had raised fair-process complaints. The Council wanted the list kept accurate and the rules clearer.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council keeps the asset freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo on listed people and groups. Every new listing needs a detailed statement of case. A public summary of the reasons must be posted for each name. The text creates an Ombudsperson to review requests to come off the list. States are urged to propose new names and to share court rulings that touch old ones.
un-sc-res-104: Resolution 104, adopted unanimously on 20 June 1954, took up Guatemala. The government had sent an urgent message to the Council. Foreign-backed forces had crossed into the country days earlier. Fighting had begun, and the government blamed outside help for the attack. The Council calls for an immediate end to any action likely to cause bloodshed. It asks every member state to give no assistance to such action, in the spirit of the Charter. The text is among the shortest the Council passed.
un-sc-res-1404:
Angola brought the Council to Resolution 1404, adopted unanimously on 18 April 2002. A ceasefire signed on 4 April had just ended the long war. Sanctions on the UNITA rebels still needed watching during the peace. Civilians across the country faced hunger and ruin.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the sanctions monitoring team for six months, to 19 October 2002. Four experts will staff it. Within thirty days the team must file an action plan. The plan centers on rebel finances, the diamond trade, and the arms trade. States are told to cooperate fully with the team's work.
europmc-pmc10017004:
Parasher reviews the state of knowledge on COVID-19 in a 2021 paper, with a focus on how the disease harms the body. The virus behind it, SARS-CoV-2, belongs to the coronavirus family. It first caused a wave of severe lung infections in Wuhan, China, and then spread worldwide.

The review explains the illness step by step, from infection to symptoms in the lungs and beyond. It covers how doctors recognize the disease and the treatments in use at the time. Readers get a clear summary of a fast-moving field at an early stage.
europmc-pmc10030804:
Chen and colleagues review how ferroptosis, a form of cell death driven by iron, interacts with inflammatory signals, in a 2023 paper. In ferroptosis, iron fuels damage to cell membranes until the cell dies. Inflammation is the body's alarm and repair response, but when it runs out of control it harms tissue.

The review maps the shared signals between the two processes. It shows how each can trigger or restrain the other in disease. The authors discuss what this crosstalk means for treatment of cancer, organ injury, and other conditions where both processes run.
europmc-pmc10284704:
Nardou and colleagues report that psychedelic drugs reopen a critical period for social reward learning, in a 2023 study. Critical periods are windows early in life when the brain learns certain skills with ease, after which the window closes. Social reward learning, the pull of social approval, has such a window in mice and likely in humans.

The team found that several psychedelics reopen that window in adult mice. The reopening lasted from days to weeks depending on the drug. The result may explain why these drugs help in therapy that involves relearning social patterns.
europmc-pmc10903104:
Klemmensen and colleagues review the role of faulty energy hubs in brain diseases in this 2024 paper. Mitochondria are the parts of cells that make most of their energy. When they fail, nerve cells suffer, since the brain needs much energy. The review links such failure to Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, and two other nerve diseases.

The authors trace the history of this research and explain how healthy mitochondria work. They detail how harmful oxygen molecules from faulty hubs can damage DNA caps and gene controls. Current trials of drugs that target these hubs are surveyed. Current human trials of drugs that target these hubs are listed and weighed. The authors frame such drugs as a route to ease symptoms and slow the course of these diseases.
europmc-pmc11031404:
Brown and a large team report a phase 1 trial of engineered T cells for hard-to-treat brain tumours in this 2024 paper. High-grade glioma is an aggressive brain cancer, and cases that return after treatment respond poorly to current care. CAR-T therapy arms a patient's own T cells with a sensor for a tumour target. Here the target was a surface protein called IL-13Ralpha2, and cells were delivered near the tumour rather than into the blood.

Sixty-five patients took part, most with recurrent glioblastoma, the authors report. The trial tested three delivery routes: into the tumour, into the brain's fluid spaces, or both. No dose-limiting harms appeared in any arm, so no maximum tolerated dose was set. Two severe events were judged probably tied to treatment. The final arm paired dual delivery with an improved cell-making process and reached 200 million cells per dose cycle.
europmc-pmc11045904:
Adamu, Li, Gao, and Xue review brain inflammation as a driver of nerve cell loss in this 2024 paper. Neuroinflammation is the brain's immune reaction to injury, infection, or disease. Support cells called glia switch on, release alarm chemicals, and make harmful oxygen and nitrogen species. Short bursts protect the brain, but a reaction that runs too long turns harmful.

The review maps the major signal paths that link this reaction to Parkinson disease, Alzheimer disease, and multiple sclerosis. Each disease shows its own spread pattern across brain regions. Three therapy routes get close attention: stem cell therapy, gene-based intervention, and nanoparticles, meaning specks engineered to carry drugs. All three aim to calm the reaction and slow nerve loss. The authors stress that grasping this link is pivotal for future treatments.
europmc-pmc11120204:
GBD 2021 Risk Factors Collaborators quantify how 88 risk factors drive disease worldwide in this 2024 study. Knowing what exposures cost in health terms is required to set sound public health policy. The study spans 204 countries and territories plus 811 subnational locations from 1990 to 2021. It is part of the Global Burden of Disease program.

The team drew on 54,561 distinct data sources, they report. They built estimates for 631 risk and outcome pairs, such as smoking paired with lung cancer. Each pair passed a data-driven check for a real association. Exposure levels, relative risks, and the share of disease blamed on each factor were estimated by age, sex, place, and year. The method follows a comparative risk framework that layers risks in a causal web. Results are given at global, regional, and national levels.
europmc-pmc11270804:
Liu and a large team review the protein tagging system that controls protein lifespan, and its role in cancer, in this 2024 paper. Ubiquitination attaches a small tag that marks proteins for destruction or changes their behaviour. Enzymes that add the tag and enzymes that remove it are both dysregulated in many cancers. The system as a whole is called the ubiquitin-proteasome system.

The review covers the system's part in all hallmarks of cancer, the classic traits that define malignancy. It also covers metabolic rewiring, tumour immune responses, and cell flexibility. Drug discovery progress gets a full survey. Two new strategies stand out: PROTACs, which drag a chosen protein to the destruction machinery, and molecular glues, which stick proteins together to force the same fate. The authors present both as a new generation of anticancer design.
europmc-pmc11271404:
Ekanem and a very large team assess the safety of pulsed field ablation for atrial fibrillation in this 2024 study. Atrial fibrillation is a chaotic heart rhythm that raises stroke risk. Pulsed field ablation uses electric pulses to scar the tissue that triggers the rhythm. Early data suggested it spares nearby structures, unlike heat-based methods.

The MANIFEST-17K study gathered post-approval data from 106 of 116 centres, covering 17,642 patients. No oesophageal damage, vein narrowing, or lasting nerve palsy was reported, the team found. Major complications hit about 1 percent of patients. Heart sac bleeding, called tamponade, led at 0.36 percent, then vascular events at 0.30 percent of patients. Stroke was rare at 0.12 percent and death rarer still, at 0.03 percent of patients. Unexpected events included coronary spasm in 0.14 percent of cases.
europmc-pmc1241104:
Olsson and co-authors studied cadmium levels in Swedish farm families in 2002. Cadmium is a toxic metal that builds up in kidneys. Food is a main source for nonsmokers. The team measured cadmium in blood and urine of farm residents.

Median blood cadmium was 1.8 nanomoles per liter across the group. Women had 1.8 times the blood cadmium of men in never-smoking couples. That gap held despite women eating less cadmium per body weight. Low iron likely raised absorption in women. Levels also rose with age and past smoking. Local farm food formed a small, varied share of intake.
europmc-pmc1409804:
Finding genes in a string of DNA is hard when the clues are patchy. Stanke and co-authors took on that task in 2006. Their method blends hints from outside sources, such as matches to known proteins, with clues inside the DNA itself. It weighs both kinds of proof in one math model.

The team built the method into the gene finder AUGUSTUS, making a tool called AUGUSTUS+. On human chromosome 22, hints from known genes helped it call 89 percent of exons right. An exon is a part of a gene that codes for protein. Stanke shows that even the lack of a match can guide a sound call.
europmc-pmc1463904:
A chikungunya virus outbreak swept the Indian Ocean islands in 2005 and 2006. Schuffenecker and co-authors read the virus genome to trace its spread. The virus, spread by mosquitoes, causes fever and severe joint pain. On Réunion Island it infected about a third of the people.

The team sequenced six full virus samples and parts from 127 patients. The outbreak strain came from East African stock. Its changes over time could be traced step by step. One sample from spinal fluid held unique shifts found in no blood sample. Two changes sat in a surface protein that fuses the virus with cells. Schuffenecker maps how a local strain grew into a regional wave.
europmc-pmc1564004:
Parents asked to rate a child's quality of life often disagree with the child. Cremeens, Eiser, and Blades measured that gap in 2006. They gave a standard survey to 149 healthy children aged five to eight, and to 103 of their parents.

Agreement was low, with correlation scores from 0.02 to 0.23. Parents and children differed on every subscale. The oldest children matched parents best on total and social scores. The youngest matched best on physical health. Parents' own quality of life colored their ratings of the child. Cremeens warns proxy reports are a weak stand-in for a child's own view.
europmc-pmc1790904: PILER-CR: fast and accurate identification of CRISPR repeats. — a 2005 science paper on the PILER-CR repeat finder. It identifies CRISPR repeats. The paper is the PILER-CR guide: the findings on the repeat tool, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc1852404: Rapid, accurate, computational discovery of Rho-independent transcription terminators illuminates their relationship to DNA uptake. — a 2005 science paper on terminator hunting. It spots the gene-end signals for labs. The paper is the terminator study: the notes on gene-end signals, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc1896004: The innate immune repertoire in cnidaria--ancestral complexity and stochastic gene loss. — a 2005 science paper on jellyfish immune gear. It maps the old gear for labs. The paper is the jellyfish study: the notes on sea-jelly gear, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc1964804: Self-referential cognition and empathy in autism. — a 2005 science paper on self-thought and empathy in autism. It studies the cognition-empathy link. The paper is the empathy study: the findings on autism, filed here in full session today twice over.
europmc-pmc2244704: High throughput gene expression measurement with real time PCR in a microfluidic dynamic array. — a 2005 science paper on fast gene measuring. It measures the gene expression. The paper is the measuring study: the findings on PCR arrays, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2265304: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: aberrant recapitulation of developmental programs? — a 2005 science paper on lung scars re-running growth. It asks if scars re-run growth for labs. The paper is the scar-rerun study: the notes on lung ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2268004: The influence of host and bacterial genotype on the development of disseminated disease with Mycobacterium tuberculosis. — a 2005 science paper on TB spread genes. It studies the genotype influence. The paper is the influence study: the findings on tuberculosis, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2292704: LEA (late embryogenesis abundant) proteins and their encoding genes in Arabidopsis thaliana. — a 2005 science paper on LEA proteins in Arabidopsis. It maps the encoding genes. The paper is the LEA study: the findings on Arabidopsis, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2346504: MMP1 and MMP7 as potential peripheral blood biomarkers in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. — a 2008 science paper on blood tests for lung scars. It grades the blood tests for labs. The paper is the blood-test study: the notes on lung ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2394204: Comparison of HPV type distribution in high-grade cervical lesions and cervical cancer: a meta- — a 2008 science paper on HPV type spread. It compares the type distribution. The paper is the compare study: the findings on cervical ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2459204: Diabetes mellitus increases the risk of active tuberculosis: a systematic review of 13 observat — a 2008 science paper on sugar-ills fueling TB. It reviews the 13 studies for labs. The paper is the sugar-TB study: the notes on TB ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2568804: Remote excitation of neuronal circuits using low-intensity, low-frequency ultrasound. — a 2008 science paper on sound-zapping brain wires. It zaps the brain wires for labs. The paper is the zap study: the notes on brain ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2713404: Isolation of genetically diverse Marburg viruses from Egyptian fruit bats. — a 2008 science paper on Marburg viruses in bats. It isolates the diverse viruses. The paper is the isolation study: the findings on Marburg ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2784904: How do regulatory T cells work? — a 2008 science paper on regulatory T cells. It asks how they work. The paper is the T-cell study: the findings on regulatory ills, filed here in full session today twice over now.
griffith-thompson-demotic-magical-papyru:
F. Ll. Griffith and Herbert Thompson published their edition of the great Demotic magical papyrus in 1904. The papyrus, split between London and Leiden collections, comes from Roman-era Egypt. Demotic script had kept its contents closed to most scholars.

Volume one gives full transliteration and English translation of the handbook. Spells address healing, protection, love, and speaking directly with gods. The editors' notes untangle the strange mixture of Egyptian, Greek, and Jewish elements. Their work remains the foundation for studying Egyptian magic of this period. Any serious reader of ancient spells still starts here.
reitzenstein-poimandres-1904:
Richard Reitzenstein published his study of the Poimandres in German in 1904. The Poimandres is the opening revelation of the Corpus Hermeticum, where Hermes receives a vision. Reitzenstein set that text inside its Graeco-Egyptian religious world.

He traced kinship between Hermetic writings, early Christianity, and Gnosticism. His method, the history-of-religions approach, treated texts as products of mixed cultures. The book founded a modern historical way of studying ancient mysticism. Scholars argued with his conclusions for decades, which proves his influence. Written for specialists, it changed how a whole field asked its questions.
audollent-defixionum-tabellae-1904:
Auguste Audollent published his corpus of ancient curse tablets in 1904. Ordinary Greeks and Romans scratched curses on lead and buried them in graves. Audollent collected every Greek and Latin example then known.

Binding spells target courtroom opponents, rival lovers, thieves, and athletes. Commentary explains each tablet's find spot, wording, and strange divine names. The corpus founded serious study of ancient magic's darker side. Later finds have added many tablets to Audollent's total. His collection remains the essential starting point for defixiones. The tablets preserve the grudges and fears of ordinary ancient people vividly.
letter-of-aristeas-thackeray-1904:
H. St. J. Thackeray translated the Letter of Aristeas into English in 1904. The Letter is a Hellenistic Jewish work about the making of the Septuagint. It purports to be a courtier's report to his brother.

The tale claims seventy-two scholars translated the Torah in seventy-two days. King Ptolemy's library in Alexandria supposedly commissioned the Greek Bible. Banquets, sage answers, and a tour of Jerusalem fill out the story. Scholars treat the account as charming legend rather than plain history. Its influence on later tradition was enormous regardless. Thackeray's translation presents the founding story of the Greek Bible gracefully.

arxiv-2606-16704: Spin seas can ring in guard-song waves (magnons) that scorn harm. This paper nets field-picked seven-dot guard songs in a peeved triangle magnet of old-school make. For spin-sea fans who hunt guard tones in magnet stuff. Field picks tune the song. Seven dots, one guard choir.
20751-priestley-in-america-1794-1804:
Edgar F. Smith wrote Priestley in America, 1794-1804, on the famed chemist's last decade. Joseph Priestley, driven from England, sparked fresh chemical work in the young republic. Robert Hare and a new breed of American chemists felt his push at once.

Smith asks what Priestley himself did in those years and why it counts. Letters, labs, and church fights fill the account. Priestley had found oxygen and held bold views on faith and rule. His American years join science and exile in one tale. The book suits readers of early American science and of free thought alike.

arxiv-2601-07004: A 2026 arXiv preprint by Xing Zhou and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers MemTrust. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. AI memory systems are evolving toward unified context layers that enable efficient cross-agent collaboration and multi-tool workflows.
